instruction: I'm really scared of getting a needle.
response: It's totally okay to feel scared about needles — lots of kids feel that way, even really brave ones. Here at Children's Hospital, your care team has something called the Comfort Promise. That means they'll do everything they can to make it hurt less. They can put a special numbing cream on your skin so you barely feel anything, and they can help you sit in a cozy position — maybe on your mom or dad's lap. You could also watch a funny video or squeeze a stress ball while it happens. You don't have to be tough about it. Just tell your nurse how you're feeling and they'll help you through it.

instruction: I don't want a needle! Please no needles!
response: I hear you — needles can feel really scary, and it's okay to say that. You're not being silly at all. The nurses here know that needles are one of the hardest parts for kids, and they have special ways to help. They can use a cream that makes your skin feel sleepy so it doesn't hurt as much, and they'll let you pick something fun to look at or hold while it happens. You can also ask your mom, dad, or whoever is with you to hold your hand. Tell your nurse exactly how you feel — they really want to make it easier for you.

instruction: Will the blood test hurt a lot?
response: It's really normal to worry about that. Most kids say it feels like a quick little pinch, and then it's over before they know it. The nurses here are really good at making it as easy as possible — they can put numbing cream on your arm first so it doesn't sting, and they might let you blow bubbles or watch something on a screen to keep your mind busy. If you're feeling scared, that's completely okay. Talk to your nurse or your parent and they'll help you feel ready.

instruction: I miss my house. I want to go home.
response: I bet you do — your home is your favourite place, and it makes sense that you'd miss it. Being in the hospital can feel really different from what you're used to. But guess what? You can bring little pieces of home with you. Your family can bring your favourite stuffed animal, a blanket, or some pictures to put near your bed. And your family can visit you and stay with you too. The doctors and nurses are working hard to help you feel better so you can get home as soon as possible.

instruction: I want my own bed. This bed is weird.
response: Hospital beds do feel pretty different, don't they? They make funny noises and move in strange ways. It's totally normal to miss your own cozy bed at home. One thing that might help is having your own pillow or blanket from home — your family can bring those for you. And even though the bed is different, the people around you are here to make sure you're safe and comfortable. If something about the bed bothers you, tell your nurse — they might be able to adjust it for you.

instruction: What if my mom has to leave? I don't want to be alone.
response: That's a really understandable worry. The good news is that your mom or another family member can stay with you a lot of the time — many rooms here at Children's Hospital even have a place for a parent to sleep overnight. And even if your mom does need to step out for a little while, you won't really be alone. Your nurses check on you regularly, even during the night, to make sure you're okay. If you ever feel lonely or need something, you can press the call button and a nurse will come to you.

instruction: I'm scared to be here at night.
response: Nighttime in a new place can feel a little spooky, and that's a really normal feeling. But you're in a safe place. Your nurses are right outside and they come in to check on you through the night — that's their job, to make sure you're comfortable and safe. If your mom or dad is staying, they'll be right beside you. You can also ask for a small light to be left on, or bring your favourite stuffed animal to cuddle. If you wake up and feel worried, it's always okay to press your call button.

instruction: Why are the machines beeping? Is something wrong?
response: Great question! Those beeping sounds can seem a little alarming, but most of the time the machines beep just because they're doing their job. It's kind of like how a microwave beeps when your food is ready — it's just giving the nurses information. Sometimes it beeps because a tube moved a tiny bit or because something finished. If something were really wrong, your nurses would be right there to help. You can always ask your nurse what a beep means — they're happy to explain!

instruction: That machine looks scary. What does it do?
response: I get why it might look a little scary — hospital machines can look big and confusing! But most of them are just there to help keep an eye on you and make sure you're doing well. They're kind of like friendly robots. If there's a machine near your bed that's making you nervous, ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist to explain what it does. Once you know what it's for, it usually feels a lot less scary. You're being so brave just for asking about it!

instruction: I'm having surgery and I'm really really scared.
response: It makes total sense to feel scared before surgery. Even grown-ups feel nervous about it. Here at Children's Hospital, they have a special program where your mom or dad might be able to come into the operating room with you while you fall asleep — you can ask your care team about that. Before the surgery, you'll meet the people who will be taking care of you, and they'll explain everything that's going to happen. They might also give you something to help you feel relaxed and sleepy. You won't feel anything during the surgery. Talk to your nurse about how you're feeling — they're really good at helping kids feel braver.

instruction: I don't want to fall asleep for the operation. What if I don't wake up?
response: That's a worry some kids have, and it's okay to talk about it. The special sleep you get during an operation is very different from regular sleep — it's carefully watched over by a whole team of doctors whose only job is to make sure you're safe the entire time. They use special tools to check on you every single second. Kids wake up from this kind of sleep every single day at this hospital. Your nurse, your doctor, or a Child Life Specialist can explain more about how it works if that would help you feel better. And remember, your family will be waiting for you when you wake up.

instruction: It hurts and I don't like it.
response: I'm sorry you're hurting — that's really no fun at all. You're doing such a good job by telling someone about it. Your nurse and doctor need to know when you're in pain so they can help. Can you tell your nurse or your parent where it hurts and how much? Some kids use a number from 0 to 10, and some use faces that show how they feel. There are things your care team can do to help you feel more comfortable, so please always speak up when something hurts. You deserve to feel as good as possible.

instruction: My tummy hurts really bad. Make it stop.
response: Oh no, I'm really sorry your tummy is hurting. That sounds really uncomfortable. The most important thing you can do right now is tell your nurse or your mom or dad exactly how it feels — is it a sharp hurt or a squeezy hurt? Does it come and go? Your doctor and nurse are the ones who can help figure out what's going on and make it better. You're being so brave, and it's always the right thing to speak up about pain. Let's make sure a grown-up on your care team knows right away, okay?

instruction: I'm going to miss my friends at school.
response: Missing your friends is totally normal — they're probably missing you too! The good news is you can still keep in touch. You can use the phone by your bed to call them, and if you have a tablet or phone, you can video chat. Children's Hospital even has free Wi-Fi so you can stay connected. And when you're feeling up to it, there are activity rooms where you might meet other kids who are here too. Your friends will be so happy to see you when you're feeling better and ready to go back to school.

instruction: Am I going to fail because I'm missing school?
response: It's really smart of you to think about school, but try not to worry too much about that right now. Your most important job is to rest and get better. Your parents can talk to your teacher about what you're missing, and teachers are usually really understanding when a student is in the hospital. There are people at the hospital who can help with that too. Right now, your health comes first, and you can catch up on schoolwork when you're ready. You're not going to fall behind just because your body needs some time to heal.

instruction: I miss my dog. Can he come visit me?
response: Aw, I bet you miss your furry friend a lot! Dogs are the best cuddle buddies. At Children's Hospital, family pets usually can't come visit because they want to keep all the kids here healthy and safe. But sometimes, in really special situations, the hospital might be able to work something out — your parent can ask your care team about it. In the meantime, maybe your family can bring you a picture of your dog to put by your bed, or you could video call someone at home so you can see your pup on screen!

instruction: I don't understand why I have to stay here.
response: That's a really fair question, and it's okay to feel confused. Sometimes our bodies need extra help to feel better, and the hospital is the best place for that because it has all the special tools and people who know how to help. Your doctor and your parents can explain more about why you need to stay — it's always okay to ask them. Nothing is being hidden from you. The goal is to get you feeling good again and back home as soon as it's safe.

instruction: Why is this happening to me?
response: That's such a big question, and it's totally okay to wonder that. Getting sick or hurt isn't something you caused — it's not your fault at all. Sometimes bodies just need a little extra help. The important thing is that you're in a place full of people who really care about you and know how to help. If you're feeling sad or frustrated, you can talk to your nurse, your parent, or a Child Life Specialist. They're here to listen and to help you through this.

instruction: I don't want to take my medicine. It tastes yucky.
response: Some medicine really does taste pretty yucky — you're not wrong about that! But your medicine is working hard to help your body feel better, even if it doesn't taste great. You can ask your nurse if there's a way to make it easier — sometimes medicine can be mixed with juice or given in a different way. Taking a sip of something you like right after can help wash the taste away too. You're doing an awesome job, and every time you take your medicine, you're one step closer to feeling better!

instruction: I can't stop crying. I'm sorry.
response: Hey, you never ever have to say sorry for crying. Crying is your body's way of letting big feelings out, and that's actually a really healthy thing to do. Grown-ups cry in hospitals too — even really tough ones. Nobody here is going to think less of you for it. If you want, you can tell me or your nurse what's making you sad, or you can just let the tears come. Sometimes a good cry actually helps you feel a little bit better afterwards. You're being so brave just by being here.

instruction: I'm trying to be brave but I keep crying.
response: You know what? Crying and being brave can happen at the same time. Being brave doesn't mean you never feel scared or sad — it means you keep going even when things are hard. And that's exactly what you're doing! Every single person who works here has seen kids cry, and they all think those kids are brave too. So let those tears out if you need to. And if you want to talk about what's making you upset, your nurse, your parent, or a Child Life Specialist would love to listen.

instruction: Is my little brother okay without me at home?
response: That's really sweet that you're thinking about your brother — it shows what a caring sibling you are. Your brother is being looked after by your family at home, and I'm sure he misses you too. Maybe you could draw him a picture or send him a message to let him know you're thinking about him. And when you're feeling better and go home, he'll be so excited to see you. Right now, your most important job is to focus on getting better so you can get back to being an awesome big sibling.

instruction: I'm so bored. There's nothing to do here.
response: Being stuck in a hospital room can definitely get boring. But there are actually more things to do than you might think! Children's Hospital has activity rooms with crafts, board games, puzzles, and LEGO. There are Child Life Specialists who plan fun activities and special events. There's even a nature-themed playroom called Ashley's Backyard and a cool SMILE Room with bubble columns and fibre optic lights! Ask your nurse what's available and when you can go explore. And you can always bring your own books, games, or watch something on the entertainment site.

instruction: I don't like hospital food. I want my mom's food.
response: It's pretty normal to miss your favourite home-cooked meals — hospital food is different from what you're used to. But the kitchen here tries hard to make food that kids like, and they have lots of choices. Your parent can also bring food from home and store it in the family fridge on your unit. Just make sure to check with your nurse first, because sometimes the doctor needs you to eat a special diet to help you get better. If something about the food really bothers you, let your care team know and they'll try to help.

instruction: I don't like it when new people come in my room.
response: I understand — it can feel a little overwhelming when lots of different people come to see you, especially people you don't know. At a teaching hospital like this one, there are doctors, nurses, students, and other team members who all work together to help you. Every person who comes in is there because they care about you getting better. It's always okay to ask someone who they are and what they're doing. And if you feel uncomfortable, tell your parent or nurse — they can help.

instruction: The doctor scares me.
response: It's okay to feel that way. Doctors can seem a little serious or unfamiliar sometimes. But your doctor is on your team — their whole job is to help you feel better. Sometimes getting to know them a little helps. You could ask them a question, like what their favourite colour is or if they have any pets. Most doctors at Children's Hospital love talking to kids. And if you're really nervous, your parent or your nurse can always be right there with you when the doctor visits. You can even ask your parent to talk for you if you want.

instruction: The kid in the next bed was crying really loud. Are they okay?
response: It can be upsetting to hear another kid crying. You have a really caring heart for worrying about them. I can't tell you exactly what's going on with that child because their health information is private, just like yours is. But I can tell you that their nurses and doctors are taking really good care of them, just like your team is taking good care of you. Sometimes kids cry because they're scared or uncomfortable, and the hospital staff are great at helping with that.

instruction: The hospital smells weird. I don't like it.
response: You're right — hospitals do have a pretty unique smell! That smell usually comes from the special cleaning products they use to keep everything super clean and germ-free. It might seem strong, but it's actually a sign that people are working hard to keep you safe and healthy. Your nose will probably get used to it after a little while. And if you want, you can ask your parent to bring something that smells like home — like your favourite blanket or pillow!

instruction: I'm going to miss my friend's birthday party.
response: Oh, that's a real bummer. Missing something fun like a birthday party is hard, and it's okay to feel disappointed. But your friend will understand — they'd want you to get better more than anything. Maybe you could video call during the party, or your parent could help you make a card or pick out a little gift to give your friend later. And who knows — when you're better, maybe you two can have your own special celebration together!

instruction: What if I'm still here for Christmas?
response: I can see why that would be on your mind. Missing Christmas at home would be really hard. But even if you are here, Children's Hospital tries to make holidays special for kids. There are special events, activities, and lots of people who want to make sure kids here still feel the holiday magic. And your family can visit and bring some of your favourite traditions to you. Your care team is also working hard to get you better and home as quickly as possible. It's always okay to talk to your nurse or parent about how you're feeling.

instruction: I need stitches and I'm scared.
response: It's really normal to be scared about stitches. But the good news is that your doctor will use special medicine to numb the area first, so you shouldn't feel the stitches going in. It might feel like a little pinch when they numb it, but after that, most kids say it just feels like a tugging sensation. You can hold your parent's hand, look away, or watch something fun on a screen while it happens. Your nurse can help you figure out the best way to stay comfortable. You've got this!

instruction: I'm getting a cast. Does it hurt?
response: Getting a cast put on actually doesn't hurt! The material they wrap around your arm or leg starts off wet and warm, and then it gets hard as it dries. It might feel a little weird, but it shouldn't be painful. The cast is like a super-strong shield that protects your bone while it heals. You might even get to pick a colour! If anything does feel uncomfortable or too tight after it's on, make sure you tell your nurse or doctor right away so they can fix it.

instruction: I keep waking up at night and I'm scared.
response: Waking up in an unfamiliar place at night can feel really unsettling. That's completely okay. Remember, your nurses are nearby all night long, and they actually check on you during the night to make sure you're doing well. If you wake up and feel scared, you can press the call button next to your bed and someone will come. If your parent is staying overnight, they'll be right there too. Sometimes it helps to have a small light on or hold onto a comfort item from home. You're safe here, even when it's dark.

instruction: I don't feel like me.
response: Being in the hospital can make everything feel a little topsy-turvy, and it makes sense that you might not feel like your normal self right now. Your body is working really hard to get better, and that can make you feel tired, grumpy, or just kind of off. That's all normal. As you start to heal, you'll begin to feel more and more like you again. In the meantime, doing things you enjoy — like drawing, playing a game, or talking to someone you love — can help. And if this feeling really worries you, it's a great idea to talk to your parent or nurse about it.

instruction: I'm MAD. This isn't fair!
response: You're right to say how you feel — being in the hospital when you'd rather be doing other things is really frustrating. It's okay to be mad about it. Being angry doesn't make you a bad kid. It just means you're having big feelings about a tough situation. Sometimes it helps to squeeze a pillow, take some deep breaths, or draw a picture of how you're feeling. You can also talk to your parent, your nurse, or a Child Life Specialist about what's bugging you. They get it, and they want to help.

instruction: Nobody tells me what's happening. I want to know.
response: You have every right to know what's going on — it's your body! Sometimes grown-ups don't always think to explain everything to kids, but that doesn't mean you can't ask. You can tell your parent or your nurse that you want to understand what's happening and why. They can explain things in a way that makes sense. Knowing what's coming usually makes things feel a lot less scary. You're so smart for wanting to understand, and your care team should be happy to answer your questions.

instruction: My mom keeps crying. Is it my fault she's sad?
response: Oh sweetie, it's absolutely not your fault that your mom is sad. Your mom cries because she loves you so, so much and she doesn't like seeing you in the hospital. Parents worry about their kids — that's just what parents do. But her tears aren't because of anything you did wrong. You being brave and working on getting better is actually the thing that helps her the most. If it makes you feel better, you could give her a hug or tell her you love her. You two are a team!

instruction: I don't like wearing this gown. Everyone can see me.
response: Hospital gowns can feel pretty silly and uncomfortable — lots of kids feel that way about them. The gown makes it easier for your doctor and nurses to check on you and do what they need to do. But you're not stuck in it all the time. When you're just hanging out, you can ask your parent to bring comfy clothes from home, like pyjamas and slippers. And your nurse will always make sure your privacy is protected — they'll pull the curtain or close the door when they need to check on you. You can always ask for that.

instruction: Can I watch TV? I want to forget I'm here.
response: Wanting to take your mind off things is totally understandable! Children's Hospital has a patient entertainment site where you can watch live TV for free or use your own streaming accounts if you have them. Watching your favourite show can be a great way to relax and feel a little more normal. You could also ask about games, crafts, or a visit from a Child Life Specialist. Taking breaks from thinking about hospital stuff is healthy — you don't have to be focused on being a patient every minute!

instruction: I have a test tomorrow and I can't sleep.
response: It's really hard to sleep when you're nervous about something the next day. Your brain keeps thinking about it, right? That's so normal. Try taking some slow, deep breaths — breathe in through your nose like you're smelling a flower, and out through your mouth like you're blowing out birthday candles. You could also ask your parent to read you a story or play some quiet music. And remember, your care team will explain everything before the test happens. If you're still really worried, it's okay to let your nurse know.

instruction: This thing in my hand hurts. What is it?
response: That's called an IV, and it's a tiny little tube that helps get medicine or fluids into your body to help you feel better. It can feel a little sore or weird, especially when they first put it in. If it's hurting you right now, please tell your nurse right away — they need to know so they can check it and make sure everything is okay. Sometimes they can make it more comfortable or adjust it. You're being so brave for having it, and it's doing an important job helping your body heal.

instruction: I miss my bedroom. And my toys. And my routine.
response: It sounds like you're missing all the things that make your day feel normal, and that's completely understandable. The hospital has a different routine from home, but your family can bring some of your favourite things — like a special toy, a book, or a blanket — to make your space feel a little more like yours. You can also try to keep some of your normal habits, like reading before bed or brushing your teeth at the same time. And every day you're here, you're getting closer to going back to all those things you love.

instruction: I have a bandage on my face. What if kids laugh at me?
response: I understand why that worries you. But here at Children's Hospital, lots of kids have bandages, casts, and other things — it's totally normal here, and nobody thinks it's funny. Your bandage is actually a sign that you're healing, like a badge of courage. When you go back to school, most kids will probably think it's cool and want to hear your story. And real friends won't laugh — they'll be glad you're okay. If someone ever does say something unkind, you can talk to a grown-up about it. But I think you might be surprised by how nice people are.

instruction: I feel lonely.
response: Feeling lonely in the hospital is something a lot of kids experience, and it's okay to say it out loud. Even though there are people around, it's not the same as being home with your friends and family. If you're feeling up to it, you might enjoy visiting one of the activity rooms where other kids hang out — there's one with games, LEGO, and crafts on the sixth floor. You can also ask about Upopolis, which is a safe website for kids in the hospital to chat with other kids across Canada. And your family and friends can call or visit you too.

instruction: I have to get an X-ray. Will it hurt?
response: Here's the good news — X-rays don't hurt at all! You won't feel a single thing. The machine just takes a picture of the inside of your body, kind of like a camera but instead of taking a picture of your face, it takes a picture of your bones. You just have to lie still or stand still for a few seconds while it takes the picture. It's super quick. The room might look big and have some interesting equipment, but none of it touches you in a way that hurts. You've got this!

instruction: I came in an ambulance and it was really scary.
response: Ambulance rides can feel scary — with the sirens and the lights and everything happening so fast. That sounds like it was a big experience for you. But the paramedics who brought you here are really caring people, and they were there to keep you safe. Now that you're at the hospital, you're in a calm, safe place where your care team is looking after you. If that ride is still on your mind and you want to talk about how it made you feel, your parent, nurse, or a Child Life Specialist would be happy to listen.

instruction: Can my daddy stay with me tonight?
response: Lots of rooms at Children's Hospital have a place for a parent to sleep overnight — like a special chair or a small bed right next to yours. Your daddy can talk to your nurse about the sleeping arrangements on your unit. If he's able to stay, he'll be right there with you. And even if he has to go home for a little while, your nurses will be watching over you all night. You won't be alone. Just let your nurse know how you're feeling, okay?

instruction: Why can't I get out of bed? I want to play!
response: I know it's really frustrating to be stuck in bed when you just want to run around and play. Your body needs some rest right now to help it get better, and your doctor wants to make sure you're safe. But that doesn't mean you can't have any fun! There are things you can do right in your bed — like drawing, playing games on a tablet, reading, or doing puzzles. You can ask your nurse when it might be okay to get up, and a Child Life Specialist might be able to bring some fun activities to you.

instruction: My mom went to get food. What if she doesn't come back?
response: Your mom is definitely coming back — she just needs to eat so she can have energy to be with you! It's like how you need to eat to feel strong. She probably went to grab something from Tim Hortons on the second floor or the vending machines, and she'll be back before you know it. While you wait, your nurses are right here taking care of you. If you start to feel really worried, you can press your call button and a nurse can come chat with you or even help you call your mom on the phone.

instruction: When can I go home? I want to go now.
response: Wanting to go home is one of the most normal feelings in the world, especially when you've been in the hospital for a while. Your doctor is the person who decides when it's safe for you to leave, and they're working hard to get you there. It might not happen as fast as you'd like, but every day your body is getting a little better. You can ask your parent or nurse what the plan is — they can help you understand what needs to happen before you can go. Hang in there — you're doing great!

instruction: I see blood and it makes me feel dizzy.
response: Feeling dizzy when you see blood is something that happens to a lot of people — even some grown-ups! It's your body's reaction and it's nothing to be embarrassed about. If you're feeling dizzy, try lying down, closing your eyes, and taking slow deep breaths. Always tell your nurse right away if you feel dizzy or faint. They can help make sure you don't see things that bother you, and they have ways to keep you comfortable. You're doing a great job of noticing how your body feels and speaking up about it.

instruction: I saw a kid in a wheelchair. Will that happen to me?
response: It makes sense that seeing other kids with different equipment might make you wonder about your own situation. Every kid in the hospital is here for their own reason, and what's happening with one child is usually very different from what's happening with you. A wheelchair doesn't always mean something really serious — sometimes kids just use one to get around the hospital more easily. If you're worried about what might happen with your own health, the best thing to do is ask your doctor or your parent. They can answer your specific questions.

instruction: I don't want anyone to visit me. I look sick.
response: That's a completely okay feeling to have. You get to decide who visits you and when. If you're not feeling up to visitors right now, your parent can let people know that you need some quiet time. Nobody will be upset about that — the people who care about you want what's best for you. And when you are ready for visitors, they'll be happy to see you no matter how you look. Right now, your only job is to rest and get better at your own pace.

instruction: They said I'm going to a special unit. Is that bad?
response: Going to a special unit like the PCCU doesn't mean something terrible is happening — it means that the hospital wants to give you extra-close attention and extra-special care. In the PCCU, there are more nurses per kid, so you actually get even more people looking after you. Think of it like the VIP section! Your family can still be with you there. If you're worried about what it'll be like, ask your nurse or your parent to explain what to expect. Knowing what's coming usually helps it feel less scary.

instruction: It's too loud and too bright. I want it to stop.
response: Hospitals can be a lot for your senses — all the lights and sounds and people. It's okay to feel overwhelmed by it. Let's see what we can do. Your nurse might be able to dim the lights in your room, and you could ask for the door to be closed to block out hallway noise. If you have headphones, listening to music or a story can help too. There's also a room on the sixth floor called the SMILE Room that has calm lights and soothing music — you could ask if you can visit when you're feeling up to it. Tell your nurse how you're feeling so they can help.

instruction: Am I in trouble? Is that why I'm here?
response: Oh no, you are absolutely not in trouble! The hospital is not a place where people go because they did something wrong. You're here because your body needs some help, and that is not your fault at all. The doctors, nurses, and everyone here are on your team — they all like kids and they chose this job because they want to help children feel better. You haven't done anything wrong, okay? You're being really brave just by being here.

instruction: I don't want to eat. I feel sick.
response: That's okay — sometimes when your body isn't feeling well, eating is the last thing you want to do. You don't have to force it. But it's important to tell your nurse that you're feeling sick and don't want to eat, because they need to know. Your doctor and nurse can figure out the best way to help your tummy feel better. Sometimes starting with small sips of water or a tiny bit of crackers can help. Just be honest about how you're feeling, and your care team will take it from there.

instruction: What's an MRI? I heard I need one and it sounds scary.
response: An MRI is a machine that takes really detailed pictures of the inside of your body — like a super-powered camera. It doesn't hurt at all! You lie on a special table that slides into a big tube, and the machine makes some loud buzzing and knocking noises while it works. You'll get headphones or ear plugs to help with the noise, and some kids even get to listen to music. The hardest part is holding still, which is like being a statue. Your care team can tell you more about what your MRI will be like, so make sure to ask questions!

instruction: This is taking forever. I'm never getting out of here.
response: I know it can feel that way when every day seems to go by so slowly. Waiting is one of the hardest parts of being in the hospital. But your doctors are keeping track of how you're doing, and they'll let you go home as soon as it's safe. In the meantime, try to find little things to look forward to each day — a favourite show, a visit from someone you love, or a fun activity. Ask your nurse if there's a plan for when you might go home. Having something to look forward to can make the waiting a little more bearable.

instruction: I can't eat anything before my test tomorrow and I'm hungry!
response: Being hungry when you can't eat is really tough — I get it. The reason the doctor wants your tummy to be empty is to keep you safe during the test. I know that doesn't make the hungry feeling go away, but it's an important rule. Your care team can tell you exactly when you'll be able to eat again, and maybe you can plan what yummy food you want after the test is done! Think of it like the best snack ever is waiting for you on the other side. You're doing a really hard thing and that takes a lot of strength.

instruction: I miss my sister. We do everything together.
response: Being apart from your sister when you're used to doing everything together must feel really strange. She probably misses you just as much! You can keep in touch by calling her on the patient phone or video chatting if you have a phone or tablet. Maybe you could both draw pictures for each other, or she could write you a letter to read. Your parent can help set up a special time for you two to talk. And the faster you focus on getting better, the sooner you'll be back together doing all your favourite things.

instruction: Why do I have to wear this bracelet? It's uncomfortable.
response: That bracelet is actually really important — it's like your hospital ID card. It has your name, your birthday, and a special barcode on it. Every time a nurse gives you medicine or takes you for a test, they check your bracelet to make sure they have the right kid. It's one of the ways they keep you safe! I know it might feel a little annoying on your wrist, but it's doing an important job. If it's rubbing or feeling too tight, let your nurse know and they can adjust it for you.

instruction: My friends are all playing soccer without me right now.
response: It's hard to know that life is going on out there while you're stuck in here. That feeling of missing out is real, and it's okay to be sad about it. But your friends aren't forgetting about you — they're probably talking about you and hoping you feel better soon. Soccer will be there when you're ready to play again. Right now, your body needs some time to heal. Maybe when you're feeling up to it, you could send your team a video message or have them sign a card for you.

instruction: The doctor said I can go home soon but I'm nervous.
response: It's actually pretty normal to feel a little nervous about going home, even though you've been wanting to go! You've gotten used to having nurses and doctors nearby. But going home means you're doing well enough that you don't need all that extra help anymore — and that's a great thing! Your care team will give your parent all the instructions for taking care of you at home, and they'll tell you who to call if you have any questions. You're going to do great. And if you're worried about anything specific, ask your nurse before you leave.

instruction: The nurse used big words I don't understand.
response: Hospital words can sound pretty confusing — even grown-ups sometimes don't know what they mean! It's always, always okay to ask someone to explain things in a way that makes more sense to you. You could say something like, 'Can you tell me that in kid words?' Nurses and doctors are happy to explain things differently. You could also ask your parent to help translate the big words. Understanding what's happening is important, and you should never feel embarrassed about asking.

instruction: They said I need another operation. I already did one!
response: That must feel really frustrating — you already went through it once and now you have to do it again. It's totally okay to feel upset about that. But here's something that might help: you already know you CAN do it, because you did it before! You're already an expert. And your care team knows you better now too, so they can help make this time even smoother. Talk to your nurse or a Child Life Specialist about how you're feeling, and they can help you prepare. You're tougher than you think.

instruction: Everyone is so nice but I still don't want to be here.
response: That makes perfect sense — the people can be wonderful, but the hospital is still not where you'd choose to be. You can appreciate the nice nurses and doctors while also wishing you were home in your own bed. Both feelings can be true at the same time. The people here are nice because they genuinely care about kids like you, and they understand that you'd rather be somewhere else. Just keep focusing on getting better, and you'll be out of here before you know it.

instruction: The exercises hurt and I don't want to do them.
response: I hear you — exercises that make you sore are no fun at all. It's okay to say that. But those exercises are actually helping your body get stronger so you can get back to doing the things you love. Think of it like training for your favourite sport. Your physiotherapist can help adjust things if they're too painful, so make sure you tell them exactly how it feels. You can also take breaks and go at your own pace. Every little bit of effort counts, and your body will thank you later. You're doing awesome.

instruction: My dad looks really worried. That makes me scared.
response: It can be scary to see your dad looking worried. Parents worry because they love their kids so much — it's like a superpower they have. But his worry doesn't mean something terrible is happening. Most of the time, parents worry just because they wish they could take away any discomfort their kid is feeling. You could talk to your dad about how you're both feeling. And if you're scared about something specific — like a test or a treatment — ask your doctor or nurse to explain what's going on. Knowledge can help both you and your dad feel less worried.

instruction: Can I go to the playroom? I need to do something fun.
response: Wanting to do something fun is a great sign! Children's Hospital has some really cool spaces for kids. There's a School-Age Activity Room on the sixth floor with crafts, board games, puzzles, and LEGO. There's also Ashley's Backyard, which is a nature-themed playroom for younger kids. Ask your nurse if you're allowed to leave your room right now — sometimes you need permission depending on your care plan. If you can't go yet, a Child Life Specialist might be able to bring some activities to your room. Fun is important medicine too!

instruction: I just want to be a normal kid.
response: You ARE a normal kid — a normal kid who happens to be in the hospital right now. Being here doesn't change who you are. You still like the same things, you're still you, and when your body has healed up, you'll go right back to your normal life. Lots and lots of kids have hospital stays, and they go on to do all the normal kid things afterwards. This is just a chapter in your story, not the whole book. And while you're here, you can still do tons of normal kid things — play, laugh, watch shows, and hang out with people you love.

instruction: What if my test says something bad?
response: Waiting for test results can feel really nerve-wracking — the not knowing is often the hardest part. It's okay to feel anxious about it. Whatever the results say, your doctors will know what to do, and they'll explain everything to you and your family. You won't have to deal with it alone. Try not to imagine the worst thing before you even know what happened — sometimes our brains jump to scary places that aren't real. For now, try to do something that takes your mind off it, and let the grown-ups on your care team do the worrying.

instruction: There was a clown in the hallway and it surprised me.
response: Oh, that was probably Ollie! Ollie is the hospital's therapeutic clown — their job is to make kids smile and have a little fun while they're here. Some kids love meeting Ollie, and others find it surprising, especially if they weren't expecting it. If clowns aren't your thing, that's perfectly fine. But if you're curious, Ollie is really gentle and silly, not the scary kind of clown at all. You get to decide whether you want to hang out with Ollie or not. Nobody will make you.

instruction: I don't want a roommate. I want my own room.
response: Sharing a room with someone else can feel awkward, especially when you're not feeling great. The hospital tries to give people the room they want, but sometimes it depends on what's available. If sharing a room is really bothering you, your parent can talk to the nurse about it. In the meantime, your nurse can close the curtain around your bed to give you more privacy. And who knows — sometimes roommates turn out to be pretty cool. But your feelings are completely valid, and it's okay to want your own space.

instruction: I had a bad dream about the hospital.
response: Bad dreams can feel so real, especially when you're already in an unfamiliar place. I'm sorry you had a scary dream. It's actually pretty common for kids (and grown-ups) to have bad dreams when they're stressed or in a new environment. The dream isn't real, and you're safe right here. If the dream is still bothering you, talking about it with your parent or a nurse can help take away some of its power. You could also try thinking of your favourite happy place before you fall asleep tonight — like a beach, or your backyard, or somewhere magical.

instruction: Why can't the hospital be more like home?
response: I wish it could be more like home for you too. The hospital has to be set up in a certain way so doctors and nurses can do their jobs and keep everyone safe, but that doesn't mean you can't bring home to the hospital a little bit. Your family can bring your favourite blanket, pictures, books, and comfy clothes. You can keep some of your home routines, like what time you brush your teeth or what you like to do before bed. Your nurses want you to feel as comfortable as possible, so let them know what would help!

instruction: The nurses are really nice but I'm just tired of being here.
response: Being tired of the hospital is one of the most common feelings there is. Even when everyone is kind and caring, it doesn't change the fact that you want to be home living your regular life. That tiredness is completely valid. Every day might feel long, but you're getting through each one, and that takes real strength. Try to find one small good thing each day — a yummy snack, a visitor, a funny show — and hold onto it. And keep talking to your care team about how you're feeling. They care about your mood, not just your body.

instruction: Why does everyone keep washing their hands all the time?
response: Great observation! Everyone washes their hands so much because it's the number one best way to keep germs from spreading. In a hospital, keeping germs away is super important because some kids' bodies are working really hard to get better and germs could make that harder. When people wash their hands before coming into your room and when they leave, they're actually protecting YOU. You can help too by washing your hands before eating and after using the bathroom. Think of it like putting on invisible germ-fighting gloves!

instruction: I like my nurse. What if I get a different one tomorrow?
response: It's so nice that you've connected with your nurse! Nurses work in shifts, so you might have different nurses at different times. But every nurse on the team knows about you and your care plan, and they'll all be kind and take good care of you. During shift change, your nurses share information about you so the next nurse knows exactly what you need. And there's a good chance you'll see your favourite nurse again on another shift. You could even make them a drawing to say thanks when they're back!

instruction: I heard an alarm going off and it scared me.
response: Alarms in the hospital can sound really startling! But most of the time, alarms are just machines letting the nurses know that something small needs attention — like an IV bag that needs to be changed, or a sensor that moved out of place. It's kind of like a doorbell ringing. The nurses know exactly what to do when they hear those alarms. If an alarm near you goes off and it scares you, you can ask your nurse to explain what it was. Most of the time, it's nothing to worry about.

instruction: People keep telling me I'm brave but I don't feel brave.
response: You know what's funny about bravery? The people who are the bravest usually don't feel brave at all. Being brave isn't about not being scared — it's about getting through something hard even though you ARE scared. And that's exactly what you're doing every single day in the hospital. So even though you don't feel brave inside, from the outside, everyone can see just how strong you are. It's okay to not feel brave. You're still doing an incredible job, and it's okay if some days are harder than others.

instruction: The parking garage was dark and scary when we came in.
response: Parking garages can feel a bit gloomy, especially when you're already nervous about going to the hospital. But the one at Children's Hospital — Parking Lot 8 — has people around and security guards who can help if you ever feel unsafe. Next time, if the parking garage feels too much, you can ask your parent to drop you off at the main entrance first and then go park. And once you're inside the hospital, it's bright and there are friendly people ready to help. You did great getting here!

instruction: I'm afraid of dogs. What if one comes to my room?
response: That's a really good thing to mention! The therapy dogs that visit Children's Hospital through St. John's Ambulance are very gentle and well-trained, but nobody will ever force you to be around one. If you're afraid of dogs, just let your nurse know, and they'll make sure a therapy dog doesn't come to your room. Everyone has their own likes and dislikes, and the hospital respects that. Some kids love the dogs and some don't, and both are perfectly okay.

instruction: How many more sleeps until I go home?
response: That's one of the hardest questions in the hospital because sometimes even the doctors aren't sure exactly how many sleeps it'll be — it depends on how your body is doing. But you can ask your parent or nurse to check with the doctor on how things are going. Every day, your care team is watching how you're doing and thinking about the best time for you to go home. In the meantime, try to make each 'sleep' count by doing something fun or relaxing during the day. You're getting closer!

instruction: They're putting medicine in my IV. Will it hurt?
response: Most kids don't feel anything when medicine goes in through the IV — it's like invisible help flowing into your body. You might feel a cool sensation in your arm, and very occasionally some medicines can make you feel a little funny for a moment. If anything hurts or feels weird, tell your nurse right away — that's really important. But most of the time, the medicine goes in and you don't feel it at all. The IV does all the work so you don't have to get another poke. Pretty smart, right?

instruction: I had an accident in my bed. I'm embarrassed.
response: Please don't be embarrassed — this happens to a lot of kids in the hospital, way more than you'd think. Your body is going through a lot right now, and sometimes accidents just happen. The nurses are completely used to it and they won't judge you or make you feel bad at all. They'll help you get cleaned up and get fresh sheets really quickly. It's just part of being in the hospital, and there's nothing to feel ashamed about. You're handling a lot, and you're doing a great job.

instruction: I want to talk to someone but I don't know who.
response: I'm really glad you want to talk to someone — that takes courage. There are lots of people here who would love to listen. You could talk to your parent or whoever is with you, or tell your nurse how you're feeling. There are also Child Life Specialists at Children's Hospital who are specially trained to help kids work through big feelings, and they're really kind. If you want, you could even express yourself through art or music therapy. You don't have to figure everything out on your own. Just saying 'I need to talk' to any grown-up here is a perfect first step.

instruction: I heard the doctors talking and they sounded serious. Am I dying?
response: Hearing doctors talk in serious voices can be really scary, especially when you don't understand everything they're saying. Doctors use their serious voice a lot because they're concentrating and being careful — it doesn't mean something terrible is happening. The most important thing is to talk to YOUR doctor or your parent about what you heard and what you're worried about. They will be honest with you and explain things in a way you can understand. Please don't keep this worry inside — the grown-ups on your team are there to answer your questions.

instruction: I forgot my teddy bear at home. I need him.
response: Oh no — I know how important a special comfort buddy can be, especially in a new place. Can you ask your parent or someone at home to bring your teddy bear on their next visit? In the meantime, the Paediatric Family Resource Centre or your nurse might have a comfort item they can lend you. It won't be exactly the same, but it might help. You could also try wrapping up in your blanket extra tight for some cozy comfort. Your teddy bear will be in your arms again soon!

instruction: My friend at school is sick too. I hope they're okay.
response: That's really thoughtful of you to be thinking of your friend. It shows what a caring person you are. You're both in good hands — whether they're at a hospital or at home, there are people taking care of them just like people are taking care of you. When you're feeling better, you could make them a get-well card or call them to let them know you're thinking of them. Taking care of yourself right now is also a way of being a good friend, because you'll be there for them once you're feeling better too.

instruction: Everything is too much. I can't handle this.
response: It's okay to feel overwhelmed — there's a lot going on, and you're dealing with more than most kids your age have to deal with. You don't have to handle all of it at once. Let's take it one small step at a time. Right now, just take a few deep breaths with me. Breathe in slowly... and breathe out slowly. Good. You don't have to be strong every second. It's okay to ask for help. Tell your parent or your nurse that you're feeling overwhelmed, and they can help make things feel more manageable. You don't have to do this alone.

instruction: Nobody from my class has called me.
response: That must feel really lonely, and I'm sorry. Sometimes your friends might not know that you want them to call, or their parents might not have your hospital number. Maybe your mom or dad could reach out to your teacher and let them know it would cheer you up to hear from your classmates. A lot of times, classes will make cards or send messages once they know you'd like that. Your friends haven't forgotten you — they might just not know the best way to reach you right now. You're definitely not forgotten.

instruction: They said I can't bring my toy into the MRI room!
response: I know that feels unfair, especially when your toy helps you feel safe. The MRI machine uses a really strong magnet, so certain things can't come inside the room — it's not about the rules being mean, it's about keeping you safe. But your toy will be right outside waiting for you, and you'll get it back the second you're done. You might also be able to bring a different comfort item that's safe for the MRI room. Ask your nurse or the MRI team what you can bring in. They really do want you to feel as comfortable as possible.

instruction: I'm scared to eat because I threw up before.
response: That makes total sense — nobody wants to throw up again, and it's smart to be cautious. Your nurse and doctor know about this and they'll tell you when it's a good time to try eating again. When you do try, they'll probably start you off with something really gentle, like small sips of water or crackers. You don't have to eat a big meal right away. Go at your own pace and let your care team know how your tummy is feeling. They're the experts at helping your tummy feel ready again.

instruction: Will I have to come back to the hospital again?
response: That's a question your doctor is the best person to answer, because it depends on what's going on with your health. Some kids come to the hospital once and don't come back, and some kids come back for check-ups or treatments. But no matter what, the hospital isn't a scary place — it's a place that helps you. And if you do have to come back, you'll already know what to expect, which makes it much easier. Ask your doctor about the plan so you're not left wondering. Whatever happens, you'll handle it.

instruction: I don't like when people I don't know touch me.
response: That's a completely reasonable feeling, and it's really important that you said it out loud. Your body is yours, and it's okay to feel uncomfortable when someone you don't know touches you. In the hospital, the doctors and nurses do need to examine you sometimes, but they should always explain what they're going to do first and ask if you're ready. If someone doesn't do that, you or your parent can remind them. You can also ask to have your parent right next to you during any exam. Speaking up about what makes you uncomfortable is always the right thing to do.

instruction: What if something is really really wrong with me?
response: I understand that scary feeling when you don't know exactly what's going on with your body. The not-knowing part is really hard. But here's the thing: your doctors are working to figure out exactly what's happening so they can help. That's what all those tests and check-ups are for. Whatever they find, they'll know what to do about it, and they'll explain everything to you and your family. You won't be left in the dark. Talk to your parent or your doctor about your worries — they're the best people to give you answers. You don't have to carry that worry alone.

instruction: My nurse helped me feel better when I was crying. I want to say thank you.
response: That's so wonderful that you want to thank your nurse! You could tell them directly — nurses love hearing that they made a difference. You could also draw them a picture or write a little thank-you note. There's even a way for your family to officially recognize a team member through the hospital's Great Moments program — your parent can fill out a form on the website to let the hospital know how special that nurse is. What a kind and thoughtful thing for you to want to do. That nurse is lucky to have a patient like you!

instruction: They said they have to do the test again because it didn't work. I don't want to!
response: Oh, I can really understand how frustrating that feels. You already got through it once, and hearing you have to do it again is really disappointing. It's okay to feel annoyed and upset. But the doctor needs the test to work properly so they can help you the best way possible. Your care team will do everything they can to make it go smoothly this time. Talk to your nurse about what happened and what they can do differently to make it easier. And remember — you've already proven you can do it. You're stronger than you know.

instruction: Will I look different after my surgery?
response: That's a really good question and it's totally natural to wonder about it. The answer depends on what kind of surgery you're having, so the very best person to ask is your doctor. They can explain exactly what to expect. Many surgeries don't change how you look at all, and even if there is a small scar, it usually gets smaller and lighter over time. Your doctor will be honest with you. And no matter what, you'll still be YOU — the same awesome person, inside and out.

instruction: I'm nervous about being in the hospital. I've never stayed overnight before.
response: A first overnight stay in the hospital is a big deal, and feeling nervous about it is completely understandable. The unfamiliarity is usually the hardest part. Here's what to expect: your room will have a bed, and many rooms have space for a parent or caregiver to stay overnight too. Nurses check on you regularly, even through the night, so you're never really on your own. You can bring your own clothes, chargers, headphones, and comfort items from home. There's free Wi-Fi and a patient entertainment site for streaming. Once you settle in, it usually feels less intimidating than you imagined. If anything worries you, just talk to your nurse — they do this every day and they're genuinely here to help.

instruction: I have a serious needle phobia. I literally cannot do this.
response: Needle phobia is really common and it's a real thing — you're not being dramatic. The staff at Children's Hospital take it seriously, and they have specific strategies to help. They can apply a topical anesthetic cream to numb the area beforehand so you feel less, and they can help you find a comfortable position. Distraction techniques like watching something on your phone or doing breathing exercises genuinely work for a lot of people. Let your nurse know how intense your fear is — they won't judge you, and they may be able to adjust the approach. You're allowed to feel scared AND get through it.

instruction: I have exams coming up and I'm stuck here. I'm going to fail everything.
response: Academic pressure on top of a hospital stay is incredibly stressful, and I hear you. But your school is required to work with you when you're dealing with a medical situation — that means accommodations, extensions, and alternative testing arrangements. Your parents can contact your school to explain the situation, and the hospital has people who can help coordinate that transition. The Transitions in Care team at Children's Hospital actually supports students moving between school and hospital. Your health has to come first right now, and no exam is more important than that. You won't fail because of a medical situation — there are systems in place to protect you.

instruction: I feel so isolated. Everyone's living their life and I'm stuck here.
response: That feeling of watching life continue without you from a hospital bed is genuinely painful. It's a loss, even if it's temporary, and it's okay to grieve that. But you're not as cut off as it might feel. The hospital has free Wi-Fi, you can use your phone, and the patient phones allow free local calling. You could FaceTime your friends, stay active on group chats, or even have visitors — up to two people can be at your bedside at a time. If you're here for a while, there's also Upopolis, a secure social platform for patients aged 8–18 to connect with other kids across Canada. You haven't been erased from your life. This is a pause, not an ending.

instruction: I hate how I look right now. The hospital gown, the IV, everything.
response: Feeling uncomfortable with how you look in this context is really valid. Hospital gowns aren't exactly designed for self-expression. When you're not in an active procedure, you can absolutely wear your own clothes — ask your nurse when that's okay. Having your own comfy hoodie or pyjamas can make a surprising difference to how you feel. The IV and medical equipment are temporary tools, not part of who you are. If body image is something that weighs on you beyond just the hospital aesthetic, there are psychologists and social workers here you can talk to confidentially. You don't have to tough it out alone.

instruction: I feel like I have zero privacy here. People keep walking in.
response: Having your privacy disrupted is frustrating, especially as a teenager when privacy matters a lot. In a hospital, staff do need to check on you, but you have every right to ask them to knock, to close the curtain, or to give you a minute to get ready. If you're sharing a room, the curtain partition is there for you — use it. During nursing shift changes (around 6:45–7:30 a.m. and p.m.), things can be a bit busier. For more sensitive conversations, there are quiet rooms on the unit that can be used for privacy. Don't hesitate to tell your nurse what you need. Your comfort and dignity matter here.

instruction: My parents are missing work and spending money on parking because of me. I feel terrible.
response: That guilt is a sign of how empathetic you are, but I want you to hear this clearly: you are not a burden. Your parents are here because you matter more to them than work schedules or parking fees. That said, there are things that might ease your mind — the hospital has parking passes that can reduce costs, and there are social workers on staff who can help families navigate financial resources. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre can help with that too. If this guilt is weighing on you, it might help to actually talk to your parents about it. They'd probably want to know how you're feeling.

instruction: I'm so angry. Why do I have to deal with this? None of my friends do.
response: That anger is completely justified. There's nothing fair about dealing with a health issue when your peers don't have to, and you don't have to pretend you're okay with it. Feeling angry doesn't make you ungrateful or difficult — it makes you human. What matters is having somewhere to channel it. Some people find it helps to write it down, talk to someone, or even just name the feeling out loud. If the anger starts to feel overwhelming or constant, the hospital has psychologists and social workers who work specifically with teens. You don't have to process this alone, and you don't have to be positive all the time.

instruction: I'm having surgery tomorrow and I can't stop thinking about it.
response: Pre-surgery anxiety is one of the most common things hospital staff see, and there's no shame in it. Here's what might help: Children's Hospital has a Parental Presence at Anaesthesia Induction program, which means a parent might be able to be with you in the operating room until you're asleep. Before surgery, the anaesthesia team will explain exactly what's going to happen. You'll be asleep the whole time, you won't feel anything, and a team of specialists monitors you every second. If the anxiety is really intense, talk to your care team — there are things they can offer to help you feel calmer. Write down your questions so you don't forget them. Knowledge is usually the best antidote to fear.

instruction: I'm back again. I'm so tired of this being my life.
response: Coming back to the hospital again when you've already been through it is exhausting — physically and emotionally. It's okay to be fed up. Living with a condition that brings you back here takes a kind of resilience that most people your age don't have to develop. That doesn't make it easier, but it does make you stronger than you probably give yourself credit for. If you're feeling burned out, that's worth talking about with your care team, a psychologist, or a social worker. The Bravery Beads program can also help you visualize your journey and acknowledge everything you've been through. You're not just 'back again' — you're still fighting, and that matters.

instruction: I'm worried my friends will forget about me while I'm here.
response: That worry is understandable, especially when your friends are together and you're not. But real friendships don't dissolve because of a hospital stay. Your friends are probably thinking about you more than you realize. Stay connected however you can — text, video calls, social media. If you're comfortable with it, let them visit. Up to two people can be at your bedside during visiting hours. You might be surprised how much your friends want to be there for you. And if anyone does pull away, that says more about them than about you. Focus on the people who show up.

instruction: I'm waiting for test results and I'm terrified of what they'll say.
response: Waiting for results is its own kind of torture — the uncertainty is often worse than the answer. Your brain is probably running through every worst-case scenario right now, and that's a normal stress response, not a prediction. Whatever the results show, your medical team will have a plan. You won't be left alone with bad news and no direction. If you're spiraling, try a grounding technique: name five things you can see, four you can hear, three you can touch. It won't erase the anxiety, but it can turn the volume down. And when the results come, make sure you ask every question you have. You deserve full information.

instruction: Nobody at school understands what I'm going through.
response: You're probably right — most of your classmates haven't had this experience, and that can feel incredibly isolating. It's hard when people say things like 'at least you get to miss school' and have no idea what you're actually dealing with. Connecting with people who do understand can help. Upopolis is a secure social network for hospital patients aged 8–18 where you can talk with other young people across Canada who get it. The hospital also has group programs and a psychology service. You don't have to educate everyone around you or justify your experience. Finding even one person who understands can make a real difference.

instruction: I hate having to ask permission for everything. I'm not a little kid.
response: That frustration is completely valid. Being a teenager is about gaining independence, and the hospital environment can feel like it strips that away — someone else controls when you eat, when you sleep, who comes in your room. It can feel infantilizing. Here's the thing, though: you still have agency here. You can advocate for yourself, ask questions, participate in decisions about your care, and set boundaries around your space and privacy. The staff here should treat you as a partner in your care, not just a patient. If you feel like you're not being heard, say so. Your voice matters, and good care teams will respect that.

instruction: I'm going to miss prom because of this. I've been looking forward to it all year.
response: That's a real loss, and I'm sorry. Missing a milestone event like prom because of something completely out of your control is heartbreaking. You're allowed to be upset about it — don't let anyone tell you it's 'just a dance.' If there's any chance the timing works out, talk to your care team about your discharge timeline. If it doesn't work out, maybe your friends can video you in, or you can plan something special of your own when you're better. The disappointment is real, but this moment doesn't define your high school experience. You have a lot of life ahead, and this is one chapter of it.

instruction: I was already dealing with anxiety before this. Being here is making it so much worse.
response: That sounds really tough. A hospital stay can amplify existing anxiety significantly — the loss of control, the unfamiliar environment, the medical uncertainty. It makes sense that you're struggling. The important thing is to not ignore it. Let your care team know about your pre-existing anxiety, because it's relevant to your care and there are things they can do to help. Children's Hospital has paediatric psychologists on staff who specifically help young people cope with the emotional side of hospitalization. You can also ask for a social worker. Managing your mental health alongside your physical health isn't optional — it's essential. Please speak up about this.

instruction: I don't want anyone posting about me being in the hospital.
response: You have every right to control that narrative. Your health information and your image are your own, and you get to decide who knows what. If you're worried about a family member or friend posting, tell them directly. Most people will respect that once they know it matters to you. The hospital also takes your privacy seriously — staff aren't allowed to share your information without consent. If someone does post something you didn't authorize, you can ask them to take it down. You're not being controlling — you're protecting your boundaries, and that's a mature and healthy thing to do.

instruction: I'm worried the hospital won't respect my pronouns.
response: That's a valid concern, and I want you to know that Children's Hospital has a Gender Pathways Service specifically for gender-diverse and transgender patients. You can let your care team know your correct name and pronouns, and they should use them. If someone on staff makes a mistake or doesn't respect your identity, you can speak to your nurse, a social worker, or contact the Gender Pathways Service directly at gps@lhsc.on.ca. You shouldn't have to fight for basic respect during a hospital stay. The hospital's job is to care for the whole you, and that includes your identity.

instruction: I don't see the point anymore. Everything just keeps getting worse.
response: I hear you, and I want you to know that feeling this way is a signal that you need more support, not that things are truly hopeless. When you're dealing with a lot of pain, frustration, or a long hospital stay, it can narrow your view until it feels like nothing will get better. That feeling is real, but it's not the whole picture. Please talk to someone you trust — your parent, your nurse, or a social worker. Children's Hospital has paediatric psychologists who are trained to help with exactly these kinds of feelings. You don't have to carry this alone, and reaching out isn't weakness. It's the strongest thing you can do right now.

instruction: I keep crying in front of the nurses and I feel so stupid.
response: Crying in the hospital doesn't make you stupid — it makes you a person dealing with a genuinely hard situation. Nurses see patients cry every day, and they don't think less of anyone for it. Holding everything in doesn't make you tougher; it just means the pressure builds up with nowhere to go. If you want privacy when you're emotional, that's okay — you can close the curtain or ask for a moment. But please don't apologize for having feelings. The staff here understand, and most of them chose this career because they care about people during their most vulnerable moments.

instruction: I'm going to lose my spot on the team. I've worked so hard for this.
response: I can only imagine how frustrating that is. You've put in real work, and the idea of losing your position because of something you can't control is gut-wrenching. Talk to your coach if you haven't already — most coaches understand medical situations, and many will hold a spot or find a way to keep you involved. Your physiotherapist at the hospital can also help you understand your timeline for returning to activity. This isn't the end of your athletic journey. Athletes deal with setbacks, and coming back from something like this can make you mentally tougher. But right now, your body needs to heal first.

instruction: I can't eat what I want. They've got me on some special diet and it's terrible.
response: Hospital diets can be really restrictive, and when food is one of the few comforts you have, losing that is rough. Your diet is prescribed by your doctor for a medical reason, so it's important to follow it even when it's frustrating. That said, the hospital offers a range of dietary options — including halal, kosher, vegetarian, and options for allergies — so there may be more choices than you realize. Talk to your care team or a dietitian about what you can eat. Your family can also bring food from home and store it in the family fridge on your unit, as long as your care team approves. Hang in there.

instruction: What if this changes my life forever?
response: That's a heavy question, and it makes sense that you'd be thinking about it. The honest answer is that your doctor is the person who can talk to you about long-term outcomes for your specific situation. Some health events are temporary, others require ongoing management, and both are livable. What I can tell you is that whatever happens, you will adapt. People — especially young people — are remarkably resilient. And you won't have to figure it out alone. There are medical teams, counsellors, and support systems built for exactly this. Please have this conversation with your doctor. You deserve honest answers, not spinning scenarios in your head.

instruction: I can't sleep here. It's too noisy and people keep coming in.
response: Hospital sleep is notoriously terrible, and you're not imagining it. Between the beeping monitors, hallway noise, and regular check-ins, getting proper rest is a real challenge. There are some things that can help: bring headphones and use a white noise or sleep sounds app, ask your nurse if the lights can be dimmed, wear an eye mask, and request that non-urgent checks be consolidated when possible. The nursing staff does need to check on you during the night for safety, but they'll try to be quick and quiet. Let your nurse know that sleep is a real issue — they deal with this a lot and may have additional suggestions.

instruction: Why do they keep talking to me like I'm five? I'm sixteen.
response: That's frustrating, and you shouldn't have to deal with that. You're a young adult and you deserve to be spoken to accordingly. Some staff may default to a younger communication style because they work with a wide age range, but that doesn't make it okay. You can say something like, 'I appreciate you explaining that, but I'd like the full details — you can talk to me like an adult.' Most professionals will adjust immediately once they realize. You're entitled to understand your own health in real terms. Advocating for how you want to be treated is an important skill, and this is a good time to use it.

instruction: Everyone's moving forward with university applications and I'm falling behind.
response: The pressure of life milestones continuing while you're dealing with a health situation is incredibly stressful. But universities understand medical circumstances, and gap years or delayed applications are far more common than you think. Your school guidance counsellor can help with accommodations and documentation. The Transitions in Care team at Children's Hospital also supports young people navigating these kinds of life transitions. Your timeline doesn't have to match everyone else's, and a few weeks or months won't derail your future. Take care of your health now — the rest will follow.

instruction: I'm in pain all the time and I'm tired of telling people about it.
response: Pain fatigue — being tired of your own pain and tired of reporting it — is a real thing, and I'm sorry you're experiencing it. But please keep communicating with your care team about your pain levels. They can't help if they don't know, and you deserve proper pain management. The Comfort Promise at Children's Hospital means they're committed to addressing your pain with evidence-based strategies. There's also the Paediatric Symptom Management and Supportive Care team, which specializes in exactly this. You shouldn't have to just endure it. Ask your nurse specifically about a pain management referral if what you're getting isn't working.

instruction: I'm worried my boyfriend/girlfriend will break up with me because of all this.
response: That's a real worry, and I understand why your mind goes there. Being in the hospital can make you feel vulnerable in all your relationships, including romantic ones. The best thing you can do is be honest with your partner about what you're going through and what you need from them. A good partner will step up. If they don't, as painful as that would be, it tells you something important about the relationship. Right now, your energy needs to go toward healing. The people who matter will still be there. And if this is weighing on you, talking to a social worker or psychologist here could help you process it.

instruction: I feel like I have no control over anything in my life right now.
response: That loss of control is one of the hardest parts of being hospitalized, and it's even harder when you're at an age where you're supposed to be gaining more independence. While you can't control your medical situation, there are things within your control: you can ask questions and participate in care decisions, choose what you eat within your diet options, decide when to have visitors, keep up with your own routines. Reclaiming even small choices can help. If this feeling of helplessness is becoming overwhelming, please talk to someone — a psychologist or social worker here can help you find strategies for coping.

instruction: The medication makes me feel weird and foggy. I don't like it.
response: Feeling foggy or not like yourself from medication is really unsettling, and it's valid to dislike it. You should absolutely tell your doctor or nurse about these side effects — there may be alternative medications, different dosages, or timing adjustments that can help. You don't have to just accept it. Your care team needs to know how medications affect you in order to find the right balance between managing your condition and your quality of life. Never stop taking a prescribed medication on your own, but always speak up about how it's making you feel. Your experience matters in these decisions.

instruction: When I go back to school, everyone's going to ask questions and I don't want to explain.
response: You get to decide how much or how little you share. You're under no obligation to explain your health to anyone. It can help to have a simple go-to response ready, like 'I had a health thing but I'm doing better now' and leave it at that. You could also ask a close friend to help deflect questions. If you're worried about the transition back to school, the Transitions in Care team at Children's Hospital specifically helps with that. Some schools can also brief teachers without going into detail. You control your story. Practice your response beforehand so it feels natural.

instruction: My sister gets to live a normal life while I'm here. It's not fair.
