response: That resentment is a natural response to an unfair situation. It doesn't make you a bad sibling. Watching someone your age live freely while you're confined to a hospital bed is painful in a way that's hard to articulate. Your feelings are valid. At the same time, your sister might be dealing with her own complicated feelings — worry, guilt, or helplessness. Illness affects the whole family differently. If this resentment is building up, talking to a psychologist or social worker can help you work through it without it damaging your relationship. You're allowed to feel what you feel.

instruction: I keep asking myself 'why me?' and I can't find an answer.
response: That's one of the most human questions there is, and the hard truth is that there isn't usually a satisfying answer. Illness doesn't target people who deserve it. It's random, and that randomness can feel maddening. You didn't do anything to cause this. Some people find that instead of answering 'why me,' it helps to shift toward 'what now' — not because the question isn't valid, but because it's a question that has actionable answers. If this question is consuming you, talking to a spiritual care practitioner, psychologist, or someone you trust could help you process it. You don't have to figure this out alone.

instruction: I don't really feel anything anymore. I'm just... numb.
response: Emotional numbness can be your mind's way of protecting you when there's too much to process. It's not weakness or being broken — it's a coping mechanism. But if it persists, it's worth paying attention to. You might be experiencing emotional exhaustion from everything you've been through. Please mention this to your care team. Children's Hospital has psychologists who work with teens specifically, and they can help you work through what you're feeling — or not feeling. There's no wrong way to react to a difficult situation, but you deserve support through all of it.

instruction: I'm going to have a scar and I hate it.
response: Concerns about scarring are completely normal, especially when your body image matters to you. Your surgeon or doctor can talk to you about what to expect in terms of healing and what the scar will likely look like over time — many scars fade significantly. There may also be treatments that can minimize scarring, so it's worth asking. Beyond the physical, if you're struggling with how a scar makes you feel about your body, that's something a psychologist here can help with. A scar tells a story about something you survived. That's not nothing. But your feelings about it are yours to have.

instruction: My parents are hovering and it's driving me crazy. I need space.
response: That tension between needing your parents and needing your independence is already real at your age — and a hospital stay dials it up to eleven. Your parents are probably in overdrive because they're scared and don't know how else to help. Try having an honest conversation: acknowledge that you know they're worried, and then explain what you actually need — maybe it's some alone time during the day, or having them step out during certain check-ups. Most parents respond well when they know what helps. You can also talk to your nurse about facilitating that conversation if it feels too hard to do directly.

instruction: I'm bored out of my mind. There's literally nothing to do.
response: Hospital boredom is real, and it can make everything feel worse. Here are some options you might not know about: there's free Wi-Fi, a patient entertainment site for streaming, and your own phone works here. But beyond screens — the hospital has art therapy, music therapy, and a School-Age Activity Room with games and crafts on the sixth floor. There's also the SMILE Room in B6-261 with sensory equipment. Child Life Specialists can connect you with activities, and if you're into martial arts or mindfulness, the Heroes' Circle program visits patients weekly. Ask your nurse what's happening this week. There's more going on than it seems from your room.

instruction: I feel like nobody on my care team actually listens to me.
response: Feeling unheard by the people responsible for your care is really frustrating, and you shouldn't have to accept it. You have the right to be listened to and included in decisions about your own health. Here are some things you can try: ask to speak directly with your attending physician, not just the residents. Write down your concerns so you don't forget them in the moment. You can also ask your parent to advocate alongside you. If things don't improve, the Patient Relations office is available to help — you can reach them at extension 52036. Your experience of your own body matters, and good medical care includes hearing the patient.

instruction: I'm terrified of going under anaesthesia. What if something goes wrong?
response: Fear of anaesthesia is extremely common, and the fact that you're thinking about it means you're processing things — that's healthy. Here's what might help: the anaesthesiologist is a specialist whose entire job is keeping you safe while you're asleep. They monitor your heart, breathing, oxygen, and blood pressure the entire time. Modern anaesthesia is very safe. Before the procedure, you'll meet the anaesthesia team, and you can ask every question you have. Children's Hospital also offers the PPI program, which may allow a parent to be with you during induction. Talk to your care team about your fear — they've supported thousands of patients through this and they can help calm your specific worries.

instruction: The food here is honestly awful. I can't eat another day of this.
response: I won't argue with you — hospital food has a well-earned reputation. But there are options. The Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B is open on weekdays until 8 p.m. There are vending machines near the Zone B elevators on the 1st and 3rd floors. Your family can bring food from home and store it in the family fridge on your unit — just check with your nurse first to make sure it fits your diet. The inpatient pantry in B6 has drinks and light snacks too. And if you have dietary preferences like halal, kosher, or vegetarian, let your care team know. It won't be gourmet, but there may be more variety than you've been offered so far.

instruction: They just told me I have a chronic condition. I don't even know how to process this.
response: A new diagnosis — especially a chronic one — can feel like the ground just shifted under you. It's okay to not know how to feel right now. Shock, denial, anger, sadness — all of those are normal responses. You don't have to process everything at once. Give yourself time. When you're ready, your care team can help you understand what this means for your daily life, and Children's Hospital has psychologists who specifically help young people adjust to diagnosis. The Transitions in Care team is also there for long-term support. This isn't the end of your story — it's a new variable in it. But right now, it's okay to just sit with the news.

instruction: I know my family can't really afford all this. It stresses me out.
response: Financial stress on top of health stress is a heavy burden, and it's mature of you to be aware of it. But I don't want this worry consuming your energy when you should be focused on healing. Here's what you should know: a lot of care at Children's Hospital is covered by OHIP, and there are social workers on staff whose job is specifically to help families navigate financial resources, insurance questions, and community support programs. There's also a legal support program called PBLO that offers free legal help to families. Encourage your parent to talk to a social worker — they can help far more than most people expect.

instruction: Nighttime is the worst. I just lie here overthinking everything.
response: Nighttime in the hospital can amplify every worry you have. Without distractions, your brain runs wild. You're not alone in that — a lot of patients struggle with nighttime anxiety. Some things that might help: listen to a podcast or calming music with headphones, try guided breathing exercises (inhale for 4 counts, hold for 4, exhale for 4), write your thoughts in a journal or your phone's notes app to get them out of your head. If the anxiety is severe or persistent, tell your nurse and ask about a referral to a psychologist. You shouldn't have to white-knuckle through every night.

instruction: My condition is embarrassing. I don't want to talk about it with anyone.
response: First, nothing about a medical condition is something to be ashamed of. But I understand that certain conditions can feel deeply personal, especially at your age. You get to set the boundaries on who knows what. With your care team, though, I'd encourage you to be as open as possible — they've seen everything, and they're bound by strict confidentiality rules. Nothing you tell a nurse or doctor leaves the room without your consent. If you're uncomfortable discussing things in front of a parent, you can ask for a private conversation with your provider. Your health depends on honest communication, and the medical staff here will never judge you.

instruction: I want to leave. Can I just sign myself out?
response: I understand you want out — hospital stays can feel suffocating. As a minor, discharge decisions involve your parents and your medical team, so you can't sign yourself out unilaterally. But your frustration deserves to be heard. Talk to your nurse or doctor about how you're feeling and ask them to explain the specific reasons you need to stay and what milestones would need to be met for you to go home. Having a clear timeline and understanding the 'why' can make the wait more manageable. If you're feeling trapped or overwhelmed, a social worker or psychologist can also help. Your feelings aren't being dismissed — but your safety comes first.

instruction: I feel like the staff forgets about me. I've been waiting forever.
response: Waiting without updates is incredibly frustrating, and you're right to feel that way. Hospital staff are often juggling multiple patients, but that doesn't mean your needs should be overlooked. Here's what you can do: press the call button and ask for an update, or ask your parent to go to the nurses' station. You can also ask for a specific timeline — 'When will someone come to check on me?' — so you're not just waiting in a void. If you consistently feel overlooked, you can speak to the charge nurse or reach out to the Patient Relations office. You deserve attentive care, and advocating for yourself is not rude — it's appropriate.

instruction: I'm going to lose my job because I can't tell them when I'll be back.
response: That's a real concern, and the financial independence that a job provides matters. If you haven't already, have your parent help you communicate with your employer about your situation. Many employers are more understanding than you'd expect, and depending on the circumstances, there may be legal protections. A social worker at the hospital can also help you understand your options. Try not to add job stress on top of health stress — right now, your primary job is recovering. You can find another position if needed, but you only get one body. Take care of it first.

instruction: I really hate being examined. It's so awkward.
response: Physical examinations can feel uncomfortable and invasive, especially during adolescence. Your feelings are completely normal. Here are your rights: a medical professional should always explain what they're going to do before they do it, you can request a same-gender provider if that makes you more comfortable, you can have a parent or nurse present (or ask them to leave), and you can ask questions at any point. No one should examine you without your understanding and cooperation. If anything during an exam makes you uncomfortable, say something. Your boundaries matter, and a good care team will respect them.

instruction: If I talk to the psychologist, does that mean something's wrong with me?
response: Absolutely not. Talking to a psychologist while you're in the hospital is like stretching when your muscles are sore — it's basic care for something that's under strain. Hospitalization is stressful. Having someone to talk to about that isn't a sign of weakness or mental illness. The paediatric psychologists here work with kids and teens every day on things like coping with being in the hospital, dealing with anxiety, adjusting to a diagnosis, and managing stress. It's confidential, it's normal, and it's there because emotional health matters. You wouldn't skip physiotherapy for a broken leg — same logic applies here.

instruction: I don't even recognize myself anymore. This whole thing has changed me.
response: Going through a significant health event can absolutely change how you see yourself and the world. That shift can be disorienting and even scary. Some of those changes might be temporary — fatigue, mood shifts, physical changes. Others might be deeper. What I want you to know is that change isn't the same as losing yourself. You're still you at your core. If you feel like you're losing touch with who you are, talking to a psychologist can help you make sense of the experience and integrate it into your identity without it taking over. Growth through adversity is real, but you don't have to navigate it alone.

instruction: I had so many plans. Now I don't know what's going to happen.
response: Having your plans disrupted by something beyond your control is deeply unsettling. You've invested in a vision of your future, and now there's uncertainty. That grief for the life you had mapped out is valid. But uncertainty doesn't mean your plans are gone — they might just need to be adjusted or delayed. Once you have more clarity on your health, you can start rebuilding. For now, try to focus on what you can control today. If the uncertainty is paralyzing you, talk to someone about it — a counsellor, social worker, or trusted adult. Planning can resume. Right now, just get through today.

instruction: They keep doing tests. How many more do I need?
response: Test fatigue is real. Every time you think it might be the last one, there's another. It can feel like your body is just a specimen. You have every right to ask your doctor why each test is being done and what they're looking for. Understanding the purpose can make it feel less arbitrary. Ask if there's a testing plan and how many more are anticipated. Informed patients feel more in control. And if a test feels unnecessary or you have concerns, speak up — you're part of the decision-making process. Your care team should be transparent with you about what's happening and why.

instruction: Some kids here seem way sicker than me. I feel guilty for complaining.
response: Pain and difficulty aren't a competition. Someone else having a harder time doesn't invalidate what you're going through. Your feelings, your fear, your frustration — they're all legitimate, regardless of what the person in the next room is dealing with. This is called 'comparative suffering' and it actually prevents people from getting the support they need. You're allowed to struggle. You're allowed to complain. And you're allowed to ask for help. Every patient here deserves the same quality of care and emotional support, including you. Don't minimize your own experience.

instruction: Why can only two people visit at a time? I want all my friends here.
response: Visitor limits exist to protect patients — including you — from overcrowding and infection, and to respect the privacy of other patients who share the space. I know it's frustrating when you want your crew around you. The current policy allows two care partners at the bedside at a time for inpatients. You could set up a rotation so different friends come at different times. Video calling is also an option for larger group hangouts. If you want to make the case for a specific exception, talk to your nurse — in some situations, flexibility is possible. The intent isn't to isolate you, it's to keep the environment safe.

instruction: I'm worried about how I'll look when I get out. I've lost weight and I look sick.
response: It's natural to be concerned about your appearance, especially when your body has been through a lot. Physical changes from illness or a hospital stay are usually temporary — once you're eating normally, moving around, and recovering, your body will start to bounce back. Your care team, including a dietitian if needed, can help with a recovery plan. If these concerns feel overwhelming or start to really affect how you feel about yourself, the paediatric psychologists here are experienced with body image and self-esteem. What your body is doing right now is surviving and healing. Give it credit for that, even when the mirror feels unkind.

instruction: My little brother is probably confused about why I'm here. I'm worried about him.
response: That shows how much you care about your family. Siblings often struggle when a brother or sister is hospitalized — they might feel scared, confused, or even a little jealous of the attention. Your parents can help by explaining the situation in age-appropriate terms and reassuring him that you're being taken care of. When you're up to it, a phone or video call could really help him feel connected to you. Some of the family support services here, including social work, can offer guidance to your parents on how to support siblings. You worrying about him shows what a great older sibling you are.

instruction: I don't want to need help for everything. It makes me feel weak.
response: Needing help isn't weakness — it's being human in a situation that demands more than one person can handle alone. You'd never think a friend was weak for needing help in the hospital, right? Give yourself the same compassion. This dependency is temporary. As you heal, you'll gradually regain your independence. In the meantime, accepting help is actually a strength — it means you're focused on recovery, not on proving something. The doctors, nurses, physios, and other staff here are specifically trained to help you get back to independence. That's the goal for everyone involved.

instruction: They keep waking me up to check my vitals. I just want to sleep.
response: I completely get how annoying that is. You finally fall asleep and then someone's there with a blood pressure cuff. The reason they do it is to catch any changes early, which can be critical for your safety — but that doesn't make it less disruptive. You can ask your nurse if the overnight check schedule can be adjusted at all, or if any checks can be combined so you get longer stretches of uninterrupted sleep. Earplugs, an eye mask, and a consistent wind-down routine can also help you fall back asleep faster after checks. Your need for rest is important, and your team knows that.

instruction: I have to use a wheelchair to get around and I feel like everyone is staring.
response: Self-consciousness about a wheelchair is really common, but in a hospital, you'll see wheelchairs everywhere — they're just a way to get around safely. Nobody is judging you for using one. If anything, people are probably wrapped up in their own concerns and barely noticing. The wheelchair is a tool that helps you move around while your body heals — it's not a statement about who you are. If it's bothering you emotionally, that's worth mentioning to a counsellor or social worker. But know that using a wheelchair right now is a practical, temporary measure, and it says nothing about your strength or your future mobility.

instruction: I haven't had a proper shower in days and I feel disgusting.
response: Feeling clean is a basic need, and not being able to shower normally can really get to you. Depending on your situation — IVs, bandages, mobility — there are workarounds. Your nurse can help you figure out the best option, whether that's a modified shower, a bed bath, or waterproof coverings for certain equipment. The sleeping areas in some units share bathrooms with showers. Ask about what's possible. If you need toiletries like shampoo, deodorant, or a toothbrush, the Paediatric Family Resource Centre or the pharmacy may have them. You don't have to just deal with it — tell your nurse, and they'll help.

instruction: I should be handling this better. Other people my age would.
response: I want to challenge that assumption. You have no idea how other people your age would handle this — most haven't had to. And the ones who have would tell you it's hard. You're not falling short of some invisible standard. There's no 'right' way to handle being in the hospital. Some days you're okay, some days you're not, and both are fine. The pressure to perform strength or resilience all the time is exhausting. Let yourself be wherever you are. If that means crying, being angry, or just being tired — that's all valid. This is hard. Full stop.

instruction: I don't fully trust the doctors here. How do I know they're making the right decisions?
response: Questioning your care team isn't disrespectful — it's your right. This is your body and your health. Children's Hospital is a teaching hospital affiliated with Western University, and the physicians here are specialists in paediatric care. That said, trust is earned, not assumed. You can ask your doctor to explain their reasoning, request information about alternative options, or ask for a second opinion. The Shared Decision Making program here encourages exactly this kind of collaboration between patients and providers. You should feel informed and involved. If you don't, raise it with your nurse, your parent, or the Patient Relations office.

instruction: I was in an accident and I keep replaying it in my head.
response: What you're describing — replaying a traumatic event over and over — is a very normal response to what you went through. Your brain is trying to process something that was shocking and overwhelming. It doesn't mean you're broken or that this will last forever. But it's really important that you talk to someone about it. The psychologists at Children's Hospital are experienced in helping young people who've been through traumatic events. You don't have to wait until you're 'worse' to ask for help. The sooner you talk about it, the better equipped you'll be to process it. Please tell your nurse or parent you'd like to speak with a psychologist.

instruction: I met a younger kid here who seems really scared. I want to help them.
response: That empathy says a lot about who you are as a person. Sometimes a kind word from someone who's been through a similar experience means more than anything an adult can say. If you see the younger kid in a shared space, a friendly smile or a simple 'hey, I know it's scary, but it gets easier' could really help. Just being visible as a teen who's handling their own hospital stay can be reassuring. You could also talk to a Child Life Specialist about volunteer or peer support opportunities. Just remember to take care of yourself first — you can't pour from an empty cup. But your instinct to help is genuinely admirable.

instruction: What if I wake up during surgery? I've heard that can happen.
response: That's a common fear, and it's been dramatized in movies far more than it reflects reality. Anaesthesia awareness is extremely rare, especially with modern monitoring equipment and the dedicated team of anaesthesiologists watching over you the entire time. They're tracking your brain activity, heart rate, oxygen levels, and more — every second. If you're concerned, bring this up directly with your anaesthesiologist before the procedure. They can walk you through the safeguards in detail. Being informed is the best way to reduce fear, and no question is too small or silly to ask your care team.

instruction: Everyone keeps telling me to stay positive and I can't do it anymore.
response: Toxic positivity in a medical setting can be exhausting. You don't owe anyone a good attitude when you're going through something this difficult. Being realistic, being frustrated, or being sad doesn't mean you're not fighting. Forced optimism can actually be counterproductive because it makes you stuff down legitimate feelings. You're allowed to have bad days. You're allowed to say 'this sucks.' The people who truly support you will accept that. If you need space from the positivity pressure, set that boundary. And if you need to talk to someone who'll just listen without trying to fix your attitude, ask for a psychologist or social worker.

instruction: I hate walking through the hospital with my IV pole. Everyone looks at me.
response: Feeling exposed while moving through public areas with medical equipment is understandable. But here's the truth: in a hospital, IV poles are as common as backpacks in a school hallway. You're not the only one walking around with one, and most people who notice aren't thinking anything negative. If it makes you feel better, you can ask your nurse about the best times to move around when hallways are quieter. You can also personalize your IV pole a bit — some patients name theirs or decorate them. But fundamentally, there's nothing to be ashamed of. You're getting treatment. That's strength, not weakness.

instruction: My phone is dead and I feel completely cut off from everything.
response: A dead phone in the hospital can feel like losing your lifeline — it's your connection to friends, entertainment, and normalcy. Ask your parent to bring a charger and maybe a portable power bank for your next visit. If you're stuck waiting, the patient phone by your bed can be used for free local and toll-free calls. The hospital also has a data valet/Wi-Fi support line if you're having connection issues. For now, see if a nurse can help you find a charger — staff sometimes have extras at the station. Staying connected is genuinely important for your mental health, and it's okay to prioritize that.

instruction: My mom hasn't slept properly in days. She won't leave my side.
response: Your awareness of your mom's wellbeing shows real maturity. Parents of hospitalized kids often push themselves to the point of exhaustion. You could try having an honest conversation: 'Mom, I'm okay here. The nurses are watching me. Please go rest.' Your care team can also encourage her. The hospital has sleeping accommodations — fold-out chairs and sleep rooms near some units — and the Ronald McDonald House nearby provides a place for families to rest. There's also the Paediatric Family Resource Centre and a sanctuary space in Zone C for quiet reflection. Taking care of herself isn't leaving you — it's making sure she can be there for you long-term.

instruction: I'm worried about getting addicted to the pain medication they're giving me.
response: That's a really thoughtful and mature concern. Addiction risk is something your care team takes seriously, and they monitor medication use carefully. Pain medication given in a supervised hospital setting for acute pain is very different from unsupervised use. If you have concerns, talk directly with your doctor or the pharmacist. They can explain what you're taking, how long you'll be on it, and what the transition plan looks like. You should never be in unnecessary pain because of fear of addiction, and you should never have unnecessary medication either. Your care team will work with you to find the right balance. Always speak up about your concerns.

instruction: I feel like all anyone sees is a patient. Not me.
response: That's a profound observation, and it's something a lot of hospitalized teens feel. When your identity gets reduced to a diagnosis or a room number, it can feel dehumanizing. You are so much more than a patient — you're a person with interests, goals, opinions, and a life outside these walls. Remind people of that. Talk about your interests, put up photos, wear your own clothes when you can. The staff here do their best to see the whole person, but you can help by bringing your personality to the forefront. And if you want to talk through this with someone, the psychologists here understand this particular kind of struggle well.

instruction: I keep telling them something feels wrong but they say my tests look fine. Am I imagining it?
response: You are not imagining it. You know your body better than anyone, and if something feels wrong, that's information worth taking seriously. 'Tests look fine' doesn't mean 'nothing is wrong' — it means the tests they've run haven't found the issue yet. Be persistent and specific about your symptoms: when they happen, how severe, what triggers them. Ask if there are other tests or specialists that could be consulted. You can also request a patient advocate through the Patient Relations office. Your voice is your most important medical tool. Don't let anyone dismiss what you're experiencing.

instruction: I don't want medical students practicing on me.
response: That's a valid concern, and you have the right to understand who is involved in your care. Children's Hospital is a teaching hospital, so medical students and residents are part of the environment. However, they always work under the supervision of experienced physicians. You can ask at any point who is doing what, and you're within your rights to request that certain procedures be performed by a senior team member. Your care team should explain who everyone is and what their role is. If you're uncomfortable with someone's involvement, speak up or have your parent advocate for you. Patient comfort is part of good care.

instruction: I had a scholarship offer for next year. I don't know if I can still take it.
response: That must feel devastating — working toward something and then having it threatened by something completely beyond your control. Before you spiral, here's what I'd suggest: most scholarship programs have processes for medical deferrals or accommodations. Have your parent contact the institution to explain the situation. A letter from your doctor can go a long way. The Transitions in Care team at Children's Hospital may also be able to support you with documentation and planning. Don't give up on that scholarship before you've explored every option. And even if adjustments need to be made, this setback doesn't erase the achievement that earned you the offer in the first place.

instruction: I complained to the nurse and now I feel bad. Am I being difficult?
response: Advocating for your own needs isn't being difficult — it's being a good patient. Nurses prefer patients who speak up about what's wrong because it helps them provide better care. If you told a nurse about pain, discomfort, a need that wasn't being met, or something that was bothering you — that's exactly what you should do. Don't confuse assertiveness with rudeness. As long as you're respectful, communicating your needs is welcomed, not resented. If you're still feeling bad about it, you could simply say to your nurse, 'Thanks for listening to me earlier.' But you truly have nothing to apologize for.

instruction: I've been Googling my condition and now I'm freaking out.
response: Dr. Google is notorious for worst-case scenarios. Medical information online is often incomplete, out of context, or written for general populations that don't match your specific situation. The best source of information about YOUR health is your actual medical team who has YOUR test results, YOUR medical history, and can answer YOUR questions. Make a list of everything you've read that worried you and bring it to your doctor. Let them address each concern with facts specific to you. Curiosity about your own health is great — just make sure you're getting your information from the people who actually know your case.

instruction: I just got my license and now I can't even walk to the bathroom on my own.
response: That contrast between the freedom you just gained and the restrictions you're now facing is genuinely jarring. Going from driving a car to needing help getting to the bathroom is a huge shift, and your frustration is completely warranted. But this is temporary. Your body is in a healing phase, and the limitations you're experiencing now aren't permanent. Physical therapists and occupational therapists here are specifically focused on getting you back to independence as quickly and safely as possible. Think of this as your body's pit stop — necessary maintenance before you're back on the road. Your license will be there when you're ready.

instruction: I'm questioning a lot of things right now — like whether any of this means anything.
response: Big life experiences like this have a way of shaking up what you thought you knew. Questioning meaning, purpose, and beliefs is not a crisis — it's a sign that you're thinking deeply about your experience. You don't have to have answers right now. If you'd like to explore these questions, Children's Hospital has a Spiritual Care service that works with people of all beliefs and backgrounds — including people who aren't sure what they believe. The sanctuary space on the third floor in Zone C is open 24/7 for quiet reflection. This kind of introspection can actually lead to real growth, even when it feels uncomfortable. Take your time with it.

instruction: Family members keep calling for updates and I just want to be left alone.
response: Caring can sometimes feel overwhelming when you're dealing with your own health. It's okay to set boundaries. You can ask your parent to be the single point of contact — one person who shares updates with the wider family so you're not fielding calls constantly. The hospital's privacy policies actually support this approach; information is only shared with parents or guardians, and they can coordinate from there. It's okay to say 'I appreciate the care, but I need quiet time right now.' Anyone who truly cares about you will respect that. Protecting your energy is part of your recovery.

instruction: What if I go home and something goes wrong and there are no nurses to help?
response: That anxiety about transitioning home is incredibly common and shows that you're thinking ahead, which is smart. Before you leave, your care team will go through detailed discharge instructions — medications, warning signs to watch for, activity levels, and who to call if something happens. If you need equipment or special care at home, an Ontario Health atHome Care Coordinator will assess that before discharge. You won't be sent home unprepared. Write down every question you have now so you can go through them before you leave. And remember, you can always call the hospital or go to the emergency department if something feels wrong. You're not being abandoned — you're being promoted.

instruction: People keep offering to help and it makes me uncomfortable. I don't want pity.
response: Distinguishing between pity and genuine care is important, and I get that it can feel blurry. Most people offering help aren't pitying you — they're just responding to a situation where someone they care about is having a hard time. Accepting help isn't admitting defeat. You can accept help while still maintaining your dignity and independence in other ways. If certain offers feel patronizing, it's okay to decline them specifically. And if you'd rather channel support in a particular way — like asking friends to send memes instead of sympathy — tell them. You get to define how people show up for you.

instruction: Last time I had this procedure it was awful. I don't want to go through that again.
response: A bad experience with a procedure leaves a mark, and it's completely reasonable to dread repeating it. But this time doesn't have to be a repeat of last time. Tell your care team exactly what happened before and what made it bad — was it pain, anxiety, communication, something unexpected? When they know specifically what went wrong, they can plan around it. Maybe they can use a different approach, offer more numbing, provide anxiety support, or simply keep you better informed. You've been through this before, which means you know what questions to ask and what to advocate for. Use that experience to make this time better.

instruction: I have a follow-up appointment in two weeks and I'm already anxious about it.
response: Anticipatory anxiety about medical appointments is very real, and it can start way before the actual event. Your brain is trying to prepare you, but sometimes it overdoes it. It might help to write down specifically what you're anxious about — is it the waiting? The potential news? A procedure? Once you name it, you can address it. If it's about information, prepare questions in advance so you feel in control. If it's about anxiety itself, ask your care team now about coping strategies you can use before and during the appointment. Two weeks is a long time to carry that weight. Don't wait until the appointment to address it.

instruction: The Wi-Fi here is so slow. It's the one thing keeping me sane.
response: I hear you — reliable internet is basically a lifeline when you're stuck in a hospital, and slow Wi-Fi makes everything more frustrating. If you're having connection issues, you can call the data valet and Wi-Fi support line for help. Sometimes switching between the available networks or moving closer to a different access point helps. You can also download content at home before a hospital visit when possible, so you have shows, music, and podcasts available offline. It's not a perfect solution, but it's a workaround. And for what it's worth, the hospital does recognize that connectivity matters for patient wellbeing.

instruction: I don't want my family to see me like this, so I pretend I'm fine.
response: Protecting your family is a loving instinct, but it comes at a cost to you. Pretending to be fine when you're not is exhausting and isolating. Your family is here because they can handle seeing you through this — that's what family does. Being honest about how you're feeling actually helps them support you better. It also models something important: that vulnerability isn't weakness. If a full emotional download feels like too much, start small. You can say something like 'I'm having a rough day' without going into every detail. You don't have to carry everything alone just to spare others. That's too much to ask of yourself.

instruction: They said I need a lumbar puncture and I'm freaking out.
response: I understand the fear — the name alone sounds intense. It's okay to be scared. What might help is knowing what to expect: your doctor will numb the area first so you shouldn't feel the procedure itself, though you might feel pressure. You'll need to stay very still, and the care team will help you get into the right position. It's usually over in 15 to 30 minutes. Talk to your doctor or nurse about exactly what to expect step by step, and ask about any comfort measures they can provide. Preparation is the best weapon against fear. And tell them you're scared — they want to know so they can support you through it.

instruction: I've gained weight from the medication and I don't feel like myself.
response: Medication-related weight changes can be really hard to deal with, especially when they change how you see yourself. Your feelings about this are valid. Talk to your doctor about the side effects you're experiencing — in some cases, there may be alternatives or adjustments. A dietitian can also help you with nutrition that supports your health without adding to the problem. Most importantly, be patient with your body. It's adapting to medication while also healing, which is a lot to ask of it. If body image is weighing on you emotionally, the psychologists here are a safe space to talk about it without judgement.

instruction: I can't do my daily prayers properly in here. It feels wrong.
response: Maintaining your spiritual practices is important, and the hospital recognizes that. There's a sanctuary on the third floor of Zone C — room C3-402 — that's available 24/7 for prayer, meditation, and quiet reflection, and it's open to people of all faiths. If you need specific accommodations — a particular direction to face, specific times, dietary requirements — let your care team know. There's also a Spiritual Care service that can help. If you're Indigenous, the Youth Indigenous Wellness Program and the Indigenous Healing Space in E1-204 may be resources for you. Your spiritual wellbeing is part of your care, and the hospital should support it.

instruction: Are my parents going to get a huge bill for this?
response: Most medical care at Children's Hospital is covered by OHIP, which means there's no bill for the core medical services. However, some things — like certain supplies, devices, or medications — may have costs that aren't fully covered. The Business Office in Zone D handles billing questions, and a social worker can help your family understand what's covered and what financial support programs might be available. There's also the PBLO legal service that helps low-income families navigate these issues. Don't carry this financial worry yourself. Encourage your parent to talk to a social worker, and let your focus stay on getting better.

instruction: I overheard another family getting bad news and now I can't stop thinking about it.
response: Overhearing something like that in a hospital is jarring, and it's natural for it to shake you. Hospitals hold both hope and heartbreak, and being surrounded by other families' journeys can affect you emotionally even when it has nothing to do with your own situation. What you heard about that family doesn't change anything about your health. If it's weighing on you, talk to someone — your nurse, a parent, or a psychologist here. Processing other people's pain while dealing with your own is a lot. Be gentle with yourself.

instruction: They keep asking me what I think about my treatment. I just want someone to decide for me.
response: Decision fatigue is real, especially when you're dealing with a health situation. It's okay to feel overwhelmed by the responsibility of participating in your care. You can tell your team that you'd like your parent or your doctor to take the lead on decisions for now. That's a valid choice. Shared decision-making is offered because your input matters, but it should never feel like pressure. When you're ready, you can re-engage in those conversations. For now, focus on healing and let the adults around you carry the decision-making load. There's no wrong way to navigate this.

instruction: I hate that two nurses are in my room talking about me during shift change. It feels invasive.
response: The bedside shift change is actually designed to include you — it's your chance to hear what's happening with your care, ask questions, and correct anything that doesn't sound right. But if it feels invasive or you'd rather not be present for it, you can tell your nurse. The handover can happen outside your room. You can also use it to your advantage: listen for information about your care plan, and speak up if something is inaccurate or if you have concerns. If the conversation feels too clinical or ignores your presence, say so. You're a participant in your care, not just the subject of a report.

instruction: They just told me I have to stay longer than expected. I can't do this.
response: Hearing that your stay has been extended when you were mentally counting down the days is crushing. That disappointment is entirely valid. Take a moment to feel it. Then, when you're ready, ask your doctor specifically why the stay was extended and what the new timeline looks like. Having concrete information helps more than vague uncertainty. You've already gotten through every day up to this point — that's proof you can keep going. Reach out to friends, ask for activities, talk to a counsellor if the news hit hard. You can do this. Not because it's easy, but because you've been doing it all along.

instruction: I know I should be grateful I'm getting help, but I mostly just feel angry and sad.
response: Gratitude and pain aren't mutually exclusive. You can appreciate the care you're receiving and still be angry about needing it. You can be thankful for your nurses and still hate being in the hospital. Those aren't contradictions — they're the full, honest range of human emotion. Nobody benefits from you suppressing the hard feelings in favour of performed gratitude. Feel what you feel. The staff here don't need you to be grateful — they need you to be honest so they can actually help you. And when you're ready, it's okay to hold both the anger and the appreciation at the same time. That's not confusing — that's real.

instruction: They said recovery will take months. I don't know how I'm going to do this.
response: A months-long recovery feels like an impossible stretch when you're standing at the beginning of it. But you don't have to do all those months today. You only have to do today. Then tomorrow. Recovery isn't a straight line — there will be setbacks and breakthroughs, and the early days are usually the hardest. As time goes on, you'll develop a routine and start seeing progress that motivates you. Your care team will be with you for this, including physiotherapists, psychologists, and social workers. Lean on your support system. You've already handled things you didn't think you could. This is no different.

instruction: I feel like they treat every patient the same. I'm not just a chart.
response: You're right — you're not just a chart, and personalized care matters. Hospital systems can feel standardized, and that can make you feel like you're on an assembly line. Speak up about your preferences, your values, your concerns. Share your interests with your care team — it helps them see you as a person. If you feel like your care lacks a personal touch, mention it to your primary nurse or a social worker. You can also share specific preferences during conversations or bedside shift changes. The best care happens when the team knows who they're caring for, not just what they're treating.

instruction: Sometimes I think about whether things will ever go back to normal.
response: That question sits with a lot of patients, especially during a long stay or a significant health event. 'Normal' might look a little different when you come out the other side — and that's okay. Some changes might actually surprise you in good ways. You might discover strength you didn't know you had, or shift what you value. And a lot of things WILL go back to how they were — friendships, interests, goals. The core of who you are isn't going anywhere. If this question is keeping you up at night, it's worth exploring with a counsellor. Not because the answer is bad, but because having someone help you think through it can make it feel less heavy.

instruction: I feel like the hospital is my whole world now. I've forgotten what outside even looks like.
response: When you're in the hospital for an extended period, the walls can start to feel like the edges of your universe. That shrinking feeling is real and it's disorienting. Try to stay connected to the outside world however you can — video calls with friends, watching content that reminds you of your normal life, looking at photos on your phone. If you're mobile enough, ask your nurse about visiting Alex's Butterfly Garden in Zone D, Level 2. It's a peaceful outdoor space with benches and a water fountain. Fresh air and a change of scenery can break the mental loop. Your world hasn't actually shrunk — your view of it just has, temporarily.

instruction: I saw them code someone down the hall. I'm really shaken.
response: Witnessing a medical emergency — even from a distance — is frightening and can leave you feeling shaken for a while. That's a completely normal reaction. The staff responding to that situation are highly trained, and the fact that there was an immediate response shows the level of care this hospital provides to every patient. What you witnessed doesn't reflect your own situation. If you're feeling anxious, scared, or just need to process what happened, please tell your nurse you'd like to talk to someone. A psychologist or social worker can help you work through that experience. You don't have to sit with it alone.

instruction: I don't want my parents reading my chart or knowing everything. I need some things to be private.
response: As a teenager, the desire for medical privacy is understandable and the hospital takes it seriously. You can talk to your nurse or doctor about which conversations you'd like to have privately. While your parents or guardians are generally included in your care because you're under 18, there are sensitive topics where your care team can respect your need for confidentiality within appropriate limits. If you're unsure about what's shared and what isn't, ask your nurse to explain. You can also speak with a social worker about navigating boundaries with your family during your stay. Your comfort with the process matters.

instruction: I don't want to be here.
response: That feeling makes complete sense — nobody chooses to be in hospital, and not wanting to be here doesn't mean anything is wrong with you. It just means you're human. The doctors and nurses here are working to help you get better so you can go home, and your feelings about being here matter. Is there anything that would make it even a little bit better right now? Sometimes just saying it out loud helps.

instruction: Everything is scary and I don't know why.
response: Sometimes our bodies feel scared even before our brains can explain why — and that's okay. Being in a new place with different sounds and smells and people can make everything feel a bit overwhelming. You don't have to know exactly what's scaring you. You can just say 'I feel scared' and someone here will sit with you. You don't have to figure it out alone.

instruction: I heard the doctor say something about my heart. What does that mean?
response: That sounds like it gave you a fright, and it makes sense that you'd want to understand. The word 'heart' in a hospital comes up a lot — doctors check heart rates, listen to heartbeats, and look at how the heart is doing as a normal part of checking how anyone is feeling. It doesn't automatically mean something serious. The best thing to do is ask your doctor or nurse directly: 'I heard you mention my heart — can you tell me what you were talking about?' You have every right to know, and they should explain it to you in words that make sense.

instruction: I just want my dog.
response: Missing your dog when you're in hospital is one of the hardest parts for a lot of kids. You can ask a family member to send you photos or videos of your dog — having them on your tablet or phone close by can really help. Children's Hospital also has therapy dogs that visit patients. Ask your nurse if you can get a therapy dog visit — it's not quite the same, but having a dog to pet can feel really comforting. Your dog will be so happy to see you when you get home.

instruction: I told my nurse I was fine but I wasn't really fine.
response: It's really common to say 'fine' when you're not — especially when you're trying to be brave or not cause trouble. But your nurses and doctors can help you better when they know how you really feel. You don't have to go into a big explanation. You could just go back and say 'Actually, I'm not that fine' and that's enough to open the door. Nobody here will think less of you for being honest about how you're doing — that's actually exactly what they need to know.

instruction: I'm scared. I'm really really scared.
response: I hear you. Being really scared is a big feeling and it's okay to feel it completely. You don't have to be calm right now. If you have a parent or family member nearby, ask them to come sit with you. If you're alone, press the call button and ask a nurse to come. You can just say 'I'm scared and I need someone here.' They'll come. You don't have to be brave all by yourself.

instruction: I've been acting fine but I'm not fine.
response: Thank you for saying that, because it takes something to admit it. A lot of people in your situation put on a face for the people around them — to protect family, to seem strong, to keep things normal. But carrying that alone is exhausting, and you don't have to. You can be honest with your nurse, a social worker, a Child Life specialist, or your care team about how you're actually doing. You don't need to explain everything perfectly. 'I've been saying I'm fine but I'm actually struggling' is enough.

instruction: I feel like I should be more scared than I am, which somehow makes me more scared.
response: That kind of meta-anxiety is real and more common than you might think. Sometimes when something serious is happening, the emotional response doesn't match what we expect — we feel numb, detached, or strangely calm — and then we start worrying about why we're not reacting 'correctly.' There's no correct way to respond to something hard. Your reaction, whatever it is, is your brain's way of managing. If it's bothering you significantly, talking to a social worker or psychologist can help you make sense of it.

instruction: I'm angry and I don't know who to be angry at.
response: Anger without a clear target is one of the most disorienting feelings that can come with being sick. It makes sense — something has happened to you that wasn't fair, that you didn't choose, that disrupted everything. There's no obvious person to be angry at, which can make the anger feel stuck. That's a completely normal part of what a lot of people go through. A social worker or counsellor can be a good space to process that kind of anger — not to get rid of it, but to understand what it's about and what to do with it.

instruction: I don't have the energy to explain how I'm feeling to one more person.
response: That makes total sense — being asked 'how are you doing?' by a new person every few hours when you're exhausted and overwhelmed is genuinely draining. You don't have to give a full account every time. 'I'm tired and I don't want to talk right now' is a complete sentence. You can also ask your nurse or a family member to pass along the key information so you're not repeating yourself constantly. And if you do want to talk at some point, you get to choose when and who.

instruction: I feel like I became a 'patient' and stopped being a person.
response: That feeling is real and a lot of people in hospital experience it — being reduced to a diagnosis, a bed number, a chart, a set of symptoms. Your identity outside this building — who you are, what you care about, what makes you you — doesn't disappear because you're here. It can help to actively hold onto those things: talking to friends, doing something you'd normally do, having your own clothes, asking people to call you by your name rather than 'the patient in room X.' If it's affecting you significantly, that's worth talking to a social worker about — they specifically help with the loss-of-self experience during illness.

instruction: My friends don't really know how to talk to me anymore since I got sick.
response: That's a really common and painful shift. Most people — especially teenagers — don't know how to talk to a peer who's dealing with something serious, so they default to avoiding the topic entirely, which can end up feeling like they're avoiding you. It usually isn't about caring less; it's about not wanting to say the wrong thing. Sometimes naming it directly helps — letting a close friend know 'you don't have to treat me differently, just talk to me like normal' can reset the dynamic. If the isolation is persistent and affecting your mental health, raising it with a social worker can help you think through it.

instruction: I've been strong for everyone else the whole time. I don't have anything left.
response: You've been carrying something really heavy for a long time, and the fact that you've been doing it for other people makes it even harder. You're allowed to put that down. You're allowed to stop managing everyone else's reactions to your situation and just focus on yourself for a bit. Telling someone 'I need to stop being the strong one for a while' is not a failure — it's honesty. A social worker or counsellor here can hold space for you to just be how you actually are, without needing to hold it together.

instruction: I keep replaying the moment I found out and I can't make it stop.
response: That kind of intrusive replay is a very common response to receiving difficult news — it's your brain processing something it hasn't fully absorbed yet. It doesn't mean you're doing something wrong. It can be exhausting and disruptive. Some things that help: writing the memory down as a way of externalizing it, talking about it with someone rather than holding it internally, and grounding techniques that bring your attention back to the present when the replay starts. If it's happening frequently and significantly affecting your ability to sleep or function, that's worth raising with a psychologist or social worker as something to address directly.

instruction: What if the nurse... I don't know, what if she hurts me?
response: It's okay that you're not sure how to ask that — it's a real fear and a lot of kids feel it. Here's what's important to know: nurses at Children's Hospital are trained to make things as gentle as possible, and you're allowed to say 'I'm scared this is going to hurt.' They'll listen. You can also ask them to stop and take a break if you need to during something uncomfortable. And if something does hurt more than it should, you can always say so — nobody is going to get in trouble because you spoke up. Your comfort and safety come first.

instruction: I feel like my parents are scared but they won't tell me why.
response: Parents often try to protect their kids from worrying by not showing how they feel — but you probably pick up on it anyway, which can actually feel scarier than knowing. If you notice your parents seem worried, it's okay to ask them directly: 'You seem worried. Can you tell me what's going on?' Most of the time, a little honesty — even about something uncertain — is less scary than the imagination filling in the blank. If they're still not telling you and you want to understand more about your situation, you can ask your doctor or nurse directly too.

instruction: Why does it have to be me?
response: That's one of the most honest questions anyone can ask, and there isn't a fair answer to it. Being sick isn't something you did wrong or something you deserved. Sometimes hard things happen to people for no reason that makes any sense. Feeling angry or sad or confused about why this is happening to you is completely understandable — those are real feelings and they matter. You're not alone in feeling that way, and you don't have to pretend to be okay with it. A Child Life specialist or social worker can be a good person to talk to when those feelings feel too big to carry.

instruction: My parents keep telling me to 'be positive' and it's making things worse.
response: That's a really common and well-intentioned thing parents say that often doesn't land the way they mean it. Being told to 'be positive' when you're genuinely struggling can feel like your real feelings aren't allowed — which makes everything harder, not easier. It might help to tell them specifically what you actually need: 'I don't need you to tell me to be positive, I just need you to sit with me' or 'I need to be able to say when I'm scared without it turning into a pep talk.' If that conversation feels too hard right now, a social worker can help you find the words.

instruction: I don't need therapy. I just want to be taken seriously.
response: That's a clear and reasonable thing to want. Being taken seriously as a teenager in a medical setting — having your pain believed, your opinions included, your preferences respected — is a basic standard of care, not a bonus. If you feel like that isn't happening, the most direct path is naming it: 'I need you to take what I'm saying seriously.' If that doesn't shift things, the charge nurse, your most responsible physician, or Patient Relations are all appropriate escalation points. You don't have to accept being dismissed.

instruction: Honestly I'm more worried about what this means for my future than what's happening right now.
response: That's a completely valid place for your mind to go — and in some ways it shows a kind of practical resilience, even if it doesn't feel that way. Questions about school, relationships, physical limitations, identity after illness, or long-term health implications are real and worth addressing. Your care team can connect you with a social worker who specifically helps with those future-facing concerns. The Transitions in Care team can also be involved if your situation has longer-term implications. You don't have to put future worries aside to focus on 'now' — both are real.

instruction: I don't know how to talk to my parents about how I'm actually feeling.
response: That's a really common challenge, especially when you're trying to protect them or when the dynamic between you is complicated by stress and fear. You don't have to start with everything. Starting small — 'I've been more scared than I've been letting on' — can open a door without it having to be a big conversation. A social worker or Child Life specialist can also help facilitate that kind of conversation if you'd rather not do it alone. Sometimes having a third person present makes it easier for everyone to say what they actually mean.

instruction: I really need someone to just sit with me right now.
response: That's a completely okay thing to need. Press the call button and when a nurse comes in, you can just say 'I'm feeling really alone and I'd like someone to stay with me for a bit.' If a parent or family member is nearby, ask them to come. A Child Life specialist can also come sit with you — their whole job is to be present for kids who need support. You don't have to explain why. Just saying you need someone is enough.

instruction: I know this sounds dumb, but I'm scared I'm going to die.
response: That doesn't sound dumb at all — it's one of the most honest fears you can have in this situation, and a lot of people in hospital feel it even when they'd never say it out loud. You're allowed to say it. If you want to understand more about your actual medical situation — what the risks are, what the outlook is — your doctor can talk to you about that directly. And if you just need someone to sit with that fear without a medical explanation, a social worker or Child Life specialist can do that too. You don't have to carry that alone.

instruction: I missed three weeks of school and I don't even know where to start.
response: Three weeks is a lot, and feeling overwhelmed about school while you're also dealing with your health is completely understandable. You don't have to figure it all out right now. Most schools have systems for extended medical absences — your parents can contact the school to let them know what's happening and ask what accommodations are available. When you're back, you don't have to catch up on everything at once. Ask your social worker here for advice on re-entry — they often have experience helping kids and teens navigate exactly this situation.

instruction: I want to go home. Not because I feel better. Just because I need to go home.
response: That's a real and human feeling, not just impatience. Being away from your own space, your own things, and your normal life for any length of time is genuinely hard. You can be honest about that with your care team — they won't dismiss it. Talk to your nurse or a social worker: 'I understand I'm not ready medically, but I need to talk about how I'm doing being away from home.' There may be things that can be done to make the time here more bearable. And if you're genuinely concerned about your readiness for discharge, that's a separate conversation worth having too.
